Thermodynamics

 Home Physics Branches of physics Statistical physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 44k Articles: 303
Thermodynamics studies energy transfers and the constraints on macroscopic changes. Its vocabulary connects internal energy, entropy, temperature, pressure and volume to heat and work. The first law of thermodynamics balances energy; the Second law of thermodynamics decides which changes can occur spontaneously and limits how much work a heat engine can deliver. These principles let us bound performance before choosing a material or a detailed machine design. Applications include power generation, propulsion and refrigerators. [ref]
Start by choosing a system boundary. A closed system can exchange energy but no matter; an isolated system exchanges neither. A state function, such as internal energy or entropy, depends on the equilibrium state. A process specifies how that state changes. Thus a body's temperature is a property it has, whereas heat records energy crossing its boundary during a process. A body contains internal energy, rather than a stored quantity of heat.
Two insulated bodies initially at different positive temperatures approach thermal equilibrium when brought into thermal contact. Their combined energy is conserved, but their combined entropy increases. They do not spontaneously separate again into a hotter body and a colder one. This familiar asymmetry makes thermodynamics interesting: conserving energy leaves many imaginable changes available, and entropy supplies a further constraint. The same distinction underlies both entropy maximization under thermal contact and the thermal efficiency limit in Carnot's theorem.

Thermodynamic system

Words: 475 Articles: 5
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A thermodynamic system is the part of the physical world selected for an energy and matter balance. Its boundary determines which transfers count as heat, work, or transported matter.

Simple compressible system

Words: 26
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
A thermodynamic system for which the reversible mechanical work is entirely pressure-volume work. At fixed composition its internal energy is specified by entropy and volume; additional work modes require additional state variables.

Thermodynamic equilibrium

Words: 371 Articles: 1
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
A thermodynamic system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when its macroscopic state has no spontaneous tendency to change through any exchange allowed by its constraints. For an isolated system, stable thermodynamic equilibrium maximizes entropy over the accessible states at fixed total energy and conserved material inventories. A wall can forbid an exchange, so always specify what can cross or move. Thermal, mechanical and chemical conditions answer different questions about that same constrained state. [ref]
For example, two compartments separated by a rigid, impermeable wall that transmits heat can reach thermal equilibrium while retaining different pressures and compositions. Allowing an unloaded piston to move adds a mechanical equilibrium condition. Allowing one chemical species to cross adds chemical potential equality for particle exchange; allowing a chemical reaction adds its chemical equilibrium condition. A fixed barrier can therefore support a constrained thermodynamic equilibrium that ceases to be an equilibrium when the barrier is removed.
Uniformity is not the definition of thermodynamic equilibrium. An isothermal atmosphere in hydrostatic equilibrium can have a common temperature while its pressure and mass density vary with height: the pressure gradient balances gravity. In an external field, the exchange condition must include the relevant potential energy; for charged matter this leads to the electrochemical potential. Relativistic gravitational corrections to thermal equilibrium are described separately by the Tolman temperature law.
A steady state only says that the macroscopic description is constant in time. A bar maintained between hot and cold thermal reservoirs has steady heat flux and produces entropy, so it is not in thermodynamic equilibrium. Even matching temperatures at one perfect-contact interface can coexist with heat transfer through the surrounding material; matching those two local values does not establish equilibrium of the whole apparatus. See thermal conduction for that spatial transport problem.
The useful simplification is that equilibrium conditions predict an endpoint without computing every collision or flow during relaxation. The first law of thermodynamics supplies the conserved quantities, and the Second law of thermodynamics supplies the direction of change. For a system held at fixed temperature and volume, the corresponding criterion is minimization of Helmholtz free energy; at fixed temperature and pressure, it is minimization of Gibbs free energy, with the material and exchange constraints still imposed.

Mechanical equilibrium

Words: 72
Thermodynamic equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Mechanical equilibrium requires force balance for the mechanical displacements that are allowed. Two uniform fluids separated by a freely moving, unloaded, frictionless piston with equal face areas require equal pressures. A supported piston can sustain a pressure difference, and a fluid in gravity instead obeys hydrostatic equilibrium. For an upward height coordinate z, that balance is dp/dz=−ρg, where ρ is mass density and g is the downward gravitational acceleration. Mechanical equilibrium alone does not establish thermal equilibrium or chemical equilibrium.

Closed system

Words: 28
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
A closed thermodynamic system exchanges no matter with its surroundings, but can exchange energy through heat or work. A sealed cylinder with a moving piston is a typical idealized example.

Isolated system

Words: 21
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
An isolated thermodynamic system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings. Its total internal energy is fixed, while the Second law of thermodynamics constrains its total entropy.

Quasistatic process

Words: 899
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A quasistatic process is an ideal limit in which a changing thermodynamic system passes through a sequence of states arbitrarily close to thermodynamic equilibrium. Its intermediate pressure, temperature and volume are therefore well defined and obey its equation of state. Driving must be slow compared with the system's own equilibration, rather than merely taking a long time on a clock. A reversible thermodynamic process additionally allows both system and surroundings to be restored without net change; friction can produce entropy even in a quasistatic process.[ref]
For a computed example, take a fixed amount of substance n of ideal gas in a sealed cylinder with a frictionless piston, in contact with a heat bath at absolute temperature T. Reduce the external load in infinitesimal steps so that the piston expands from V0​ to 2V0​. In the reversible limit, the gas pressure exceeds the external pressure by an infinitesimal amount during expansion, and the heat transfer occurs across an infinitesimal temperature difference. Exact mechanical equilibrium would give no driving force; the limiting imbalance supplies motion while preserving equilibrium intermediate states.[ref]
Along this reversible isothermal expansion, the ideal gas law gives
p(V)=VnRT​,nRT=1kJ,V0​=1L=10−3m3,p0​=V0​nRT​=1MPa.
(1)
Here R is the molar gas constant; specifying nRT fixes an energy scale, without choosing n and T separately. The initial and final equilibrium states are (V0​,p0​,T) and (2V0​,p0​/2,T). Count work delivered to the surroundings as positive. The reversible work is the shaded area beneath the pressure-volume curve:
Wout,rev​=∫V0​2V0​​p(V)dV=nRTln2≈0.693147kJ.
(2)
The integral of 1/V supplies the natural logarithm. Since internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, ΔU=0; the first law of thermodynamics, ΔU=Qin​−Wout​, gives Qin,rev​=0.693147kJ to the displayed precision. The heat bath replaces the energy delivered as work.[ref]
Now start from the same initial state, but abruptly lower the external pressure to the constant value pext​=p0​/2=0.5MPa. There is a finite initial pressure imbalance, so this is an irreversible expansion rather than a quasistatic process. Assume the piston begins and ends at rest, has no net change in stored energy, and has no external friction; relaxation occurs within the gas and its heat bath. After motion has settled and the heat bath has restored temperature T, mechanical equilibrium and the ideal gas law give Vf​=nRT/pext​=2V0​. The work delivered to the constant load is
Wout,load​=pext​(Vf​−V0​)=(0.5MPa)(1L)=0.5kJ,ΔU=0,Qin,load​=0.5kJ.
(3)
This work follows directly from load force times piston displacement, using dV=Adx for piston area A. Intermediate gas states need not have a single equilibrium pressure or temperature. In particular, neither p(V)=nRT/V at the bath temperature nor p(V)=pext​ describes the actual gas during this irreversible motion. The rectangle below plots the known external load; its upper edge is not an equilibrium gas path.
The entropy accounting makes the difference precise. Because entropy is a state function, both expansions have the same gas entropy change, computed along the reversible isothermal expansion:
ΔSgas​=∫V0​2V0​​TδQrev​​=nRln2.
(4)
The thermal reservoir stays at T and loses heat Qin​=Wout​, so ΔSbath​=−Wout​/T. Assume the ideal load stores work without an entropy change. The combined entropy production is therefore
ΔStotal​=nRln2−TWout​​={0,nR(ln2−1/2)>0,​reversible expansion,constant external load.​
(5)
No numerical entropy unit is implied by nRT=1kJ alone: nR or T must also be specified. The lost work opportunity is TΔStotal​=0.193147kJ for this comparison. This calculation uses equilibrium endpoints and the reservoir's temperature, without assigning equilibrium intermediate states to the irreversible gas. [ref]
For another boundary choice, let the same ideal gas expand into an initially evacuated compartment of volume V0​ inside a rigid, insulated vessel of total volume 2V0​. Removing the partition causes free expansion: no load is moved and no heat crosses the outer boundary, so Wout​=Qin​=0 and ΔU=0. After equilibration the temperature is again T, the pressure is p0​/2, and the gas entropy has increased by nRln2. The outer vessel has fixed volume; the gas's accessible volume doubles. Restoring the initial gas state requires compression and removal of heat, changing the surroundings. Equal endpoints do not make free expansion reversible. [ref]
A slowly moving piston with dry friction supplies a different caution: its gas can remain arbitrarily close to thermodynamic equilibrium, yet rubbing still converts work into heat and produces entropy. If the frictional force has a nonzero slow-motion limit, its dissipated energy over a fixed travel does not vanish with speed. Reversing the motion reverses friction, so infinitesimally changing the external load cannot retrace the same operation and restore the surroundings. The heat capacity calculations additionally exclude friction and other dissipative work.[ref]
The usefulness of a quasistatic process is that it replaces detailed motion by a readable sequence of equilibrium states. An equation of state and an integral then turn a pressure-volume drawing into an energy budget. The beautiful distinction is that internal energy and entropy depend on the endpoints, while heat and work record how the change was performed. Reversible benchmarks expose how much work an irreversible device sacrifices, while entropy production explains why simply making it slower need not recover that opportunity.

State function

Words: 27
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A state function depends on the current equilibrium state, rather than the path used to reach it. Internal energy and entropy are state functions; transferred heat and work depend on the process.

Heat engine

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A heat engine uses a repeating thermodynamic cycle to turn part of an incoming heat transfer into net outgoing work. In the two-thermal reservoir model, the hot thermal reservoir supplies heat Qh​>0 at fixed temperature Th​, and the cold thermal reservoir receives heat of magnitude Qc​>0 at fixed temperature Tc​<Th​. A Stirling engine makes the repeated motion visible; the abstract energy budget applies independently of its particular mechanism.[ref]
Choose the entire cyclic device as a closed system, with no net change in bulk kinetic energy or potential energy. Count heat entering as positive and net work delivered as positive, as in the first law of thermodynamics. Thus Qh​ enters with a plus sign and Qc​, although a positive magnitude, enters with a minus sign. Assume these two heat transfers and the net work are the only transfers across the boundary. Over one complete thermodynamic cycle, all stored energy, including internal energy U, returns to its starting value:
ΔU=Qh​−Qc​−W=0,W=Qh​−Qc​.
(6)
The device does not accumulate heat from cycle to cycle. More precisely, heat is a transfer, while internal energy is what can be stored; even a component that temporarily stores internal energy must return to its initial state for this boundary to be cyclic.[ref]
For engine operation, Qh​>Qc​ and W>0. Its thermal efficiency is
η=Qh​W​=1−Qh​Qc​​.
(7)
Use net work, after subtracting any work supplied during compression or required by auxiliaries included in the chosen device. For periodic operation, average power satisfies Pout​=Q˙​h​−Q˙​c​ and η=Pout​/Q˙​h​, with the rates averaged over complete thermodynamic cycles.[ref]
For a stipulated model at Th​=600K and Tc​=300K, let Qh​=1000J and Qc​=600J per thermodynamic cycle. Then W=400J and η=2/5=40%. At two thermodynamic cycles per second, these become 2000W incoming heat transfer, 1200W outgoing heat transfer, and 800W net power. These are constructed values, not measurements.
Different signs describe different tasks. With the same directions of heat transfer, Qh​=Qc​ gives W=0: a device transmitting heat without net work output. If Qc​>Qh​, net work is supplied to that device. A refrigerator or heat pump instead extracts heat from the cold side and delivers heat to the hot side, using positive input work Win​ and the balance Qh​=Qc​+Win​. Their useful output is heat transfer, measured by a coefficient of performance. Finally, a one-time isothermal expansion can have Q=W and ΔU=0 while leaving the volume changed: it is not a complete thermodynamic cycle. A warming device also fails the cyclic assumption, and a fuel-consuming device requires an accounting of matter crossing its boundary.
For two fixed thermal reservoirs at positive thermodynamic temperatures, the Second law of thermodynamics strengthens the energy balance to
η≤ηC​=1−Th​Tc​​.
(8)
Equality requires the overall operation to be a reversible thermodynamic process, including its heat transfer to the thermal reservoirs. The Carnot cycle explains how the reversible benchmark is constructed, and Carnot's theorem explains its universality and the entropy production penalty. Use kelvin values, never ratios of degree Celsius readings. The example above lies below the 50% bound: its total entropy production is −1000/600+600/300=1/3JK−1 per thermodynamic cycle.
This is useful before building a machine: warmer cooling surroundings reduce the possible thermal efficiency, even if the mechanism is unchanged. A small observed thermal efficiency does not by itself test the Second law of thermodynamics; heat leaks, friction, incomplete recovery of work, and the measurement boundary can all reduce the reported ratio. A meaningful comparison requires the actual thermal reservoir temperatures, matched heat and net work measurements, and the hypotheses of Carnot's theorem. Finite bodies whose temperatures change are treated separately there.
The practical question already appears in the 1824 Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu et sur les machines propres à développer cette puissance by Sadi Carnot: pp. 6–8 ask whether machines driven by heat have a fundamental limit and whether changing the working substance can improve their output. Pages 9–11 describe heating and cooling in real machines, but use the historical caloric theory, rather than the modern first law of thermodynamics balance. The historical discussion under Carnot's theorem explains that distinction.

Stirling engine

Words: 229 Articles: 1
Heat engine OurBigBook.com
A Stirling engine repeatedly heats and cools a confined gas, whose expansion and compression drive a moving mechanical load. This makes it a particularly accessible example of a heat engine: both the repeating motion and the two regions exchanging heat can be observed.
In the published Demonstration experiments with a Stirling engine by Christopher G Deacon and others, an electrical heater warms one end of a cylinder and flowing water cools the other at 12∘C. A moving displacer shuttles gas through copper wool that temporarily stores and returns internal energy. A laser spot traces a closed pressure-volume path on a screen: mechanical motion controls one coordinate, pressure the other. Calibrating both scales converts the enclosed area to work per thermodynamic cycle; multiplying by rotation frequency gives gas-cycle power. At 97W heater input, the paper reports 4.4W gas-cycle power, while a separate Prony brake measures 3.4W shaft output. The cold-side temperature is controlled and two higher heater settings are compared. The handout distinguishes warm-up from steady operation and asks students to compare the final warming with direct heating by the lamp. It gives a procedure, not a table of measured efficiencies. A matched run with no input estimates exchange with the room. For constant Ceff​ and no phase transition, the resulting model is
Ein​=Ceff​(Tf​−Ti​)+Qleak,out​,

where Qleak,out​ is the signed net heat lost to the room during the measurement. A heater's electrical work includes changes in its stored internal energy and heat transfer that bypasses the engine. Calorimetry

Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Calorimetry measures heat transfers. A calorimeter, a calibrated heat capacity and an accounting of unwanted heat transfer connect an observed temperature change to an energy balance, as in heat-engine calorimetry and heat-pump calorimetry.
The central idea is to measure a response that is easier to observe than the transfer itself: a known heat capacity turns a temperature change into an energy estimate. Mixing calorimetry can determine an unknown specific heat capacity, while a chemical reaction can be studied by measuring the response of its surroundings. The useful observable is a change in temperature, together with a stated thermodynamic system boundary; a hot object does not contain a separately conserved store of heat.
For a closed system with unchanged bulk kinetic energy and potential energy, let Qin​ be net inward heat and Won​ net inward work. The first law of thermodynamics gives
ΔU=Qin​+Won​.
(10)
If the boundary includes a hot sample, receiving water and the participating vessel, their mutual heat transfer is internal. With no external input, the total storage change is minus the signed outward heat leakage, not the positive amount transferred from sample to water. A calorimeter calibration with an immersed resistor instead supplies electrical work across this boundary; Joule heating converts it into internal energy. Choosing only the receiving water as the boundary changes which transfers count as external.
The mechanical constraint decides which storage quantity the readout represents. For a closed system at fixed volume, with no other work, QV​=ΔU. At constant external pressure, with only expansion work pΔV, Qp​=ΔH, where H=U+pV is enthalpy. Thus the corresponding warming balances use heat capacity at constant volume or heat capacity at constant pressure. Electrical or shaft work must be included separately when present. These endpoint balances do not require the actual exchange to be a reversible thermodynamic process.
A covered cup open to atmospheric pressure approximately realizes the second constraint when escaping material is negligible. A sealed rigid reaction vessel realizes the first; its surrounding water, vessel and immersed parts form the calibrated receiver. The reaction's outward heat equals the receiver's gain only after losses and ignition input have been accounted for. The distinction concerns the reaction boundary, even if its receiver is open to atmospheric pressure.[ref]
A historical quantitative result appears in James Prescott Joule's On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat (1850): Table IX gives 772.692 foot-pounds of mechanical work per warming of one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit, with weighing reduced to vacuum. His final rounded statement specifies water between 55 and 60 degrees Fahrenheit. He acknowledged residual vibration and sound as possible upward bias. This is an original reported conversion result, not the definition of the modern joule; the apparatus and resting controls are described in Joule's paddle-wheel experiment.[ref]

The striking feature is that the final temperature is a weighted arithmetic mean with heat capacities as weights, rather than weights given by mass. The vessel participates in the exchange even though it is not the sample being studied.
For a hot nonreacting sample of mass mx​, initial temperature Tx​ and unknown specific heat capacity at constant pressure cx​, let receiving water have mass mw​, initial temperature Tw​ and known specific heat capacity at constant pressure cw​. Let the vessel and immersed parts start at Tw​ and have combined heat capacity Ccal​, excluding that water. Assume a common final temperature Tf​, approximately constant pressure and heat capacities, no phase transition, no chemical reaction and negligible external nonexpansion work. For signed outward heat loss Qloss,out​, the combined enthalpy balance is
mx​cx​(Tf​−Tx​)+(mw​cw​+Ccal​)(Tf​−Tw​)=−Qloss,out​.
(11)

cx​=mx​(Tx​−Tf​)(mw​cw​+Ccal​)(Tf​−Tw​)+Qloss,out​​.
(12)
The loss is positive if the room receives net heat, negative if the room supplies it. If the vessel starts at a different temperature Tcal,i​, replace its warming term by Ccal​(Tf​−Tcal,i​); do not assume the vessel shared the water's initial temperature. For variable material properties, replace each mcΔT by the corresponding integral m∫cp​(T)dT and each vessel term by ∫Ccal​(T)dT. The inferred constant cx​ then represents an average over the sample's cooling interval.[ref]
For a synthetic no-loss example, mix 0.100kg of hot water at 80∘C with 0.200kg of cold water at 20∘C in a vessel initially at 20∘C. Stipulate cw​=4180Jkg−1K−1 and Ccal​=100JK−1. The enthalpy balance gives

For an unknown-sample example using the same cold water and vessel, stipulate mx​=0.100kg, Tx​=80∘C and cx​=450Jkg−1K−1. With no loss, Tf​≈22.752∘C. Inverting the full balance returns 450Jkg−1K−1; ignoring vessel storage returns about 402Jkg−1K−1. With a positive outward loss, ignoring that loss also biases the inferred cx​ downward under these hot-sample conditions. A small water temperature rise makes sensor offsets and loss estimates relatively influential; propagation of uncertainty must include the measured temperatures, masses and calibrated vessel term.

A practical receiver has an inner vessel, insulation or an outer shield, a lid, a thermometer and a stirrer. Its participating heat capacity includes the immersed parts that follow the water's temperature. These serve different purposes: a well-insulated vessel can still have substantial heat capacity, and a uniform temperature does not imply zero external heat transfer.
The University of Toronto's Heat Capacity (University of Toronto laboratory handout) describes a copper inner vessel, outer shield, thermometer and heated metal block. The inferred specific heat capacity comes from the block's cooling and the warming of both water and vessel. In its cooling exercise the handout deliberately exposes the inner vessel to room air, recommends readings every 15s, and uses the later common cooling to estimate the earlier loss. Starting below room temperature reduces exchange without guaranteeing cancellation. The handout notes limited time and thermometry for small corrections; it supplies no dataset.[ref]
For a proposed modern version, independently perform thermometer calibration and calorimeter calibration, record bath and room temperatures, and keep immersion depth, lid position and stirring rate fixed. Ensure the block actually reaches bath temperature; minimize and account for adhering hot bath water. Compare repeated transfers with different delays and a reference sample of known specific heat capacity. For mixing calorimetry, infer cooling behavior only after the sample, water and vessel approach a common temperature. Extend the model or report a limitation if sensor delay, substantial temperature gradients, changing room temperature, or escaping material invalidate that assumption. The historical caloric theory treated heat as a conserved substance. The modern first law of thermodynamics conserves energy, allowing net heat input to become work in a heat engine.

Refrigerator

Words: 384 Articles: 1
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A refrigerator removes heat from the region we want to keep cold and releases heat to warmer surroundings. Here we consider a work-driven cyclic device: its useful output is the cold-side extraction Qc​, and its input is net work W. A food compartment is a familiar example; the same cooling objective applies when removing heat from a room. The coefficient of performance measures extraction per unit work, rather than the fraction of input energy converted into output. [ref]
Choose the complete machine as the thermodynamic system. Let Qc​>0 be heat entering from the colder side, Qh​>0 be heat delivered to the hotter side, and W>0 be net work supplied, all over the same complete cycle. Assume these are its only energy transfers, no matter crosses the outer boundary, and there is no net change in stored energy. Returning to the initial state gives ΔU=0, so the first law of thermodynamics reads
0=Qc​−Qh​+W,Qh​=Qc​+W.
(18)
The heat leaving the warmer side includes both the extracted heat and the supplied work. For instance, stipulated transfers Qc​=3kJ and W=1kJ require Qh​=4kJ; the cooling coefficient of performance is 3. This is an illustrative budget, not measured performance. At steady operation the same balance holds for average transfer rates, Q˙​h​=Q˙​c​+Pin​, where Pin​ is input power.
This budget explains a useful counterexample: operating a refrigerator with its door open inside an otherwise isolated room cannot cool the room as a whole. If both heat transfers occur within the room and the electrical input comes from outside, the room gains Qh​−Qc​=W each cycle. Locally cold air does not imply net cooling. The Second law of thermodynamics permits cold-to-hot transfer because work is supplied; it forbids a cyclic device whose sole effect is that transfer. See the Clausius statement of the second law.

Refrigerator OurBigBook.com
Vapor-compression refrigeration circulates a working fluid through cold and hot coils. In the cold coil, liquid becomes gas while absorbing heat from the refrigerated region. Compression supplies work and raises the pressure and temperature; the hot coil releases heat as the gas returns to liquid. A restriction reduces the pressure before the next cold-side passage. Changing the pressure changes the temperature of the phase transition, letting one circulating fluid receive and release heat at different temperatures. This physical implementation serves both refrigerators and heat pumps; its ordinary dissipative operation differs from the reversible Carnot cycle used to bound performance. [ref] [ref]

A heat pump uses work to deliver heat to the region we want to keep warm. Its useful output is the hot-side delivery Qh​. The same operating machine can be described as a refrigerator when the cold-side extraction Qc​ is the objective: which output is useful changes the coefficient of performance, while the energy balance stays Qh​=Qc​+W. Heating a water bath by taking heat from a colder water bath makes this distinction visible in the heat-pump calorimetry experiment below. [ref]
In the illustrative budget from refrigerator, supplying 1kJ of work delivers 4kJ of useful heat, giving a heating coefficient of performance of 4. The additional 3kJ came from the colder region. Compare an ideal electrical heater whose entire input work becomes heat in the target region: it delivers 1kJ for that input. The appeal of a heat pump is this ability to move existing energy, while the Second law of thermodynamics limits the work saving for a given pair of temperatures.

To obtain temperature-only bounds, impose stronger assumptions: a cyclic machine exchanges heat only with two ideal thermal reservoirs maintained at uniform, fixed absolute thermodynamic temperatures 0<Tc​<Th​, and receives work through an ideal input carrying no entropy. Free expansion occurs when a gas spreads into an initially evacuated region without driving an external load. The standard idealization uses a rigid, insulated vessel: initially a partition confines the gas to volume V1​, while the remaining compartment contains vacuum. Open a passage and wait for thermodynamic equilibrium; the same fixed amount of substance n now occupies the larger accessible volume V2​. The outer vessel never changes size. This simple release separates three questions: what energy is conserved, whether temperature changes, and why entropy increases. [ref]
Choose the gas as the closed system, neglect heat exchange with the walls, and assume negligible changes in bulk kinetic energy and potential energy between the equilibrium endpoints. Insulation gives Qin​=0; no moving outer boundary or external load receives work, so Wout​=0. The first law of thermodynamics therefore gives

The gas can develop internal motion during the release; this does not supply external work. The intermediate state need not have one equilibrium pressure or temperature, so there is no actual quasistatic process curve p(V) to integrate. In particular, substituting the equilibrium ideal gas law into ∫pdV would describe a different process. [ref]

With positive heat capacity at constant volume, U(T2​)=U(T1​) implies T2​=T1​, and the ideal gas law gives p2​/p1​=V1​/V2​. Doubling the accessible volume thus halves the final pressure without changing the final temperature. This is an endpoint statement; it does not assert a spatially uniform, constant temperature during the rush. Insulation alone does not imply constant temperature: a reversible adiabatic expansion cools an ideal gas because it supplies work. [ref]
For a real gas, U(T,V) can depend on volume as well as temperature, so unchanged internal energy need not mean unchanged temperature. For a fixed-composition simple compressible system in a single thermodynamic phase, equilibrium identities using a Maxwell relation give
dU=CV​dT+[T(∂T∂p​)V​−p]dV,(∂V∂T​)U​=CV​p−T(∂p/∂T)V​​.

For a finite free expansion, solve U(T2​,V2​)=U(T1​,V1​), or integrate this slope along equilibrium states of equal internal energy; that mathematical curve does not describe the actual release. Free expansion is useful because it tests how internal energy depends on number density while eliminating external expansion work. Its beautiful surprise is that an ideal gas can finish with the same temperature and internal energy but greater entropy: a thermometer alone cannot diagnose reversibility. In his paper published in 1845, Joule connected two copper receivers with stopcocks, filled one with compressed dry air, and evacuated the other with an air pump. He immersed the connected receivers in water in an insulated arrangement, stirred the water, and read a sensitive thermometer. He then opened the stopcocks, let the air redistribute, stirred again, and compared the water's temperature with its initial value. Alternating control trials accounted for effects such as stirring and evaporation. The observation was no detectable net cooling of the common bath, rather than a record of the gas temperature at every instant. [ref] [ref]
Joule also immersed the receivers and their connecting piece in separate water vessels. The source receiver cooled while the receiving side warmed, with nearly cancelling thermal effects. [ref]
This distinguishes local transient changes from the final observation for the combined apparatus. Insulating its outer boundary suppresses external heat exchange; it does not prevent heat exchange between the gas, the receivers and the water inside that boundary.
An idealized modern version can use two rigid chambers joined by a valve, with thermometers in the chambers and on the walls. Prepare one chamber with gas and the other evacuated, disconnect the pump, close the apparatus to matter exchange, and let the initial temperature settle. Record initial and final equilibrium pressure and temperature, along with the wall response. Repeated closed-valve runs can reveal drift and valve-actuation effects; independent heating calibrations can estimate the heat capacity of the participating apparatus. This is a proposed measurement protocol, not a claim of a particular measured result. Fast local readings can characterize the release, but they cannot replace the final equilibrium readings in the endpoint internal energy balance.

The predicted cooling magnitude changes from 0.5K for the gas alone to 0.005K for the combined apparatus. An illustrative effective detection threshold of 0.01K would miss the latter. These are chosen numbers, not Joule's measurements. In this approximation a null observation only bounds ∣A∣≲(CV,g​+Ca​)ϵT​, where ϵT​ is the detectable temperature change after allowing for drift and other experimental uncertainties; a display's smallest digit is not automatically this threshold.

Zeroth law of thermodynamics

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Laws of thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
If two thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with the same third system in the same equilibrium state, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Write A∼B for this relation. The zeroth law of thermodynamics supplies transitivity:
A∼CandB∼C⟹A∼B.
(31)
Its symmetric relation property and self-equilibrium (reflexivity), together with transitivity, make thermal equilibrium an equivalence relation. Its equivalence classes can be labelled by a common empirical temperature; choosing an absolute numerical scale requires the further structure of thermodynamic temperature.[ref]
The comparison assumes internally equilibrated macroscopic bodies, unchanged composition and mechanical constraints, and contact permitting only heat exchange. Use rigid, impermeable diathermal walls so that neither matter transfer nor boundary work spoils the test. The same state of C matters: letting C warm while measuring A, then cool while measuring B, does not supply the premise. Ordinary nonrelativistic laboratory thermodynamics is assumed; the Tolman temperature law treats gravitational qualifications. Equal temperatures establish the thermal condition, without requiring mechanical equilibrium or chemical equilibrium.
This explains why a thermometer can compare unlike materials: it supplies a reusable third system. A temperature is a property of an equilibrium state, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Two bodies at the same temperature can have different internal energies and heat capacities. A thermometer therefore does not measure a body's stored amount of heat; the finite-body disturbance and waiting-time calculations in thermometer describe how making the comparison can change the state being measured.[ref]
The name “zeroth” reflects logical order rather than the date of the first thermometer: this premise about thermal equilibrium precedes the already numbered first law of thermodynamics, Second law of thermodynamics and Third law of thermodynamics. This is the naming explanation given in University Physics Volume 2 by Samuel J. Ling and others (§1.1, “Thermal Equilibrium”).[ref]
The corresponding Zeroth law of black-hole mechanics states constancy of surface gravity over an equilibrium horizon; Hawking radiation identifies that quantity with physical temperature up to its universal conversion factor.

Zeroth-law thermometer comparison

Zeroth law of thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Put a contact thermometer C in thermal contact with A, wait for thermal equilibrium, and record response XA​. Repeat with B under the same operating constraints. If XA​=XB​, and the calibrated response is an injective function of temperature on this range, C occupies the same thermal reference state in both comparisons. The zeroth law of thermodynamics then predicts A∼B. Equality of raw numbers from different uncalibrated thermometers supplies no such premise.[ref]
Use a probe whose participating heat capacity is small relative to each sample, or use maintained heat baths. Otherwise the matching readings describe the disturbed final states. Also hold the probe's immersion and mechanical conditions fixed: its response can depend on more than temperature. Matching readouts only tests agreement within resolution and repeatability, rather than proving exact equality of temperatures.
Agreement within a tolerance is not itself an equivalence relation. With a 0.10∘C tolerance, readings 25.00 and 25.16∘C each agree with 25.08∘C, yet disagree with each other. This is a limitation of the measurement rule, not a failure of the exact transitivity asserted by the zeroth law of thermodynamics.

Stipulate two equilibrated reference baths whose corrected thermometer readings are 0∘C and 40∘C, in degree Celsius units. Suppose the corresponding column heights are 12mm and 52mm. These are constructed inputs, not observed measurements. Assume the response is linear over this interval, with the same immersion and reading procedure throughout. Applying thermometer calibration gives
∘CtC​(X)​=4052mm−12mmX−12mm​.
(32)
For X=37mm, first subtract the zero-reference height, then divide by the full reference span: (37−12)/(52−12)=25/40. Multiplying by the 40∘C span gives tC​=25∘C, or T=298.15K in kelvin. Thus equal 37mm readings in separately equilibrated samples test equal temperatures, regardless of how much internal energy those samples contain. The Celsius offset and modern absolute-scale definition are described in degree Celsius and kelvin.
The two endpoints determine the assumed line, but do not establish linearity. An independent middle reference and a return to the initial bath can test curvature and drift. If the height has an error of 0.2mm while reference values and endpoints are held exact in this calculation, the inferred temperature error is 0.2∘C; that is only the height contribution, not a full measurement error budget. A boiling-water reference needs a measured atmospheric pressure correction, rather than an automatic 100∘C assignment. The modern kelvin is not defined by either bath.
Reference-bath thermometer comparison
Words: 291
Zeroth-law thermometer comparison OurBigBook.com
A motivating real procedure is NIST's ambient thermometer verification. Its apparatus is a deep beaker of water, a calibrated reference thermometer, a test thermometer, and a magnetic stirrer with any heater switched off. Let the water approach room temperature, stir gently, immerse both sensing tips well below the surface, and wait before reading. NIST specifies about 20cm of water, 10–15cm immersion where possible, and an initial five-minute wait. Record test then reference, repeat in reverse order, and apply the reference's certificate correction. Subtract corrected reference from test: the difference estimates the test instrument's error at this bath temperature. Agreement between the two reading orders checks repeatability. [ref]
For example, suppose a test reads 24.7∘C, a reference reads 24.4∘C, and its certificate says to add 0.1∘C. The corrected reference is 24.5∘C, so the test error is +0.2∘C: it reads high. These are illustrative readings. This verification tests a previously calibrated instrument at one point; it does not establish the two-point response used in two-point thermometer calibration example.
Additional controls follow from the thermal equilibrium premise. Keep tips away from walls and bottom, interchange probe positions to test a temperature gradient, and check that longer waits and modest immersion changes leave agreement unchanged within the required tolerance. A flat trace alone can be a steady state maintained by competing heat transfer paths. Five minutes is a procedural starting point, not a universal equilibration time. Excessive stirring can supply work and warm the bath, while probe stems can exchange heat with the room. These controls test whether both probes sample the same state; neither one-point agreement nor this experiment proves the zeroth law of thermodynamics for every material and condition.

Its units are inverse pressure, Pa−1; its reciprocal KX​=1/κX​ is the constrained bulk modulus, measured in pascal units. Holding temperature fixed gives isothermal compressibility; holding entropy fixed gives isentropic compressibility κS​ along an isentropic process. The latter describes a reversible adiabatic compression, since an irreversible adiabatic process can increase entropy. [ref]
For an ideal gas, the ideal gas law PV=NkB​T and the reversible ideal-gas adiabat give, at the same equilibrium state,

Constant γ is required for the finite-path formula PVγ=constant. Reversible adiabatic compression raises the temperature, making the pressure rise more steeply than in an isothermal compression. Thus keeping entropy fixed makes the gas harder to compress locally. For a classical monatomic gas at 100kPa, γ=5/3, so κT​=10−5Pa−1 and κS​=6×10−6Pa−1; the corresponding values of the bulk modulus are 100kPa and 166.67kPa.

where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion. The ideal gas result is one example of this broader link between mechanical and thermal responses. The equality κT​=κS​ is possible when α=0 and the other responses remain finite. These formulas compare equilibrium partial derivatives, rather than arbitrary fast or dissipative compression histories. [ref]

Take one mole of classical monatomic gas, with stipulated molar gas constant R=8.314Jmol−1K−1, initially at T0​=300K and P0​=100kPa. The initial volume is V0​=nRT0​/P0​=0.024942m3. Compressing to V0​/2 gives
Isothermal:Reversible adiabatic:​P2​=2P0​=200kPa,T2​=300K,P2​=25/3P0​≃317.48kPa,T2​=22/3T0​≃476.22K.​

κT​=−V1​(∂P2∂2G​)T,N​.

This follows from V=(∂G/∂P)T,N​, with G denoting Gibbs free energy. Within a stable single thermodynamic phase, increasing pressure reduces volume and makes this curvature negative. At phase coexistence, changing the phase fraction can change the volume at constant temperature and pressure; the usual finite single-phase isothermal compressibility then need not exist. Maxwell relations turn pressure, volume and temperature measurements into information about entropy. For example, the pressure rise when heating a rigid sealed vessel determines the entropy change when expanding the same sample isothermally:
(∂V∂S​)T,N​=(∂T∂P​)V,N​.
(38)
The quantities on the two sides describe different experiments, yet both are mixed partial derivatives of one Helmholtz free energy. This is the useful surprise: a mechanical measurement can reveal a thermal property. Similarly, the coefficient of thermal expansion gives (∂S/∂P)T,N​=−αV. [ref]
For a simple compressible system, hold particle number N and composition fixed, and allow only pressure-volume work. Write U for internal energy, H=U+PV for enthalpy, F=U−TS for Helmholtz free energy, and G=H−TS for Gibbs free energy. Their natural-variable differentials are
dU(S,V,N)dF(T,V,N)​=TdS−PdV,=−SdT−PdV,​dH(S,P,N)dG(T,P,N)​=TdS+VdP,=−SdT+VdP.​
(39)
Thus the first partial derivatives, with the subscript recording the variables kept fixed, are
US​​V,N​=T,FT​​V,N​=−S,​UV​​S,N​=−P,FV​​T,N​=−P,​HS​​P,N​=T,GT​​P,N​=−S,​HP​​S,N​=V,GP​​T,N​=V.​
(40)
The symmetry of second derivatives produces all four standard Maxwell relations, including their signs:
U:(∂V∂T​)S,N​H:(∂P∂T​)S,N​F:(∂V∂S​)T,N​G:(∂P∂S​)T,N​​=−(∂S∂P​)V,N​,=(∂S∂V​)P,N​,=(∂T∂P​)V,N​,=−(∂T∂V​)P,N​.​
(41)
For a brief derivation of the F relation, differentiate FT​=−S with respect to V and FV​=−P with respect to T: −SV​=FTV​=FVT​=−PT​. Each other row follows in the same way. Assume continuous second partial derivatives of the relevant thermodynamic potential in the region considered. At a phase transition, the equilibrium potential may lose this smoothness; apply the identities within each smooth thermodynamic phase, and handle latent heat and phase coexistence separately. If particle numbers vary, the potential differentials acquire chemical potential terms, so the fixed-N constraints must remain explicit. [ref]
For an ideal gas with fixed N, the ideal gas law gives P=NkB​T/V. At fixed volume, heating changes the pressure at rate NkB​/V. Consequently an isothermal expansion at positive temperature has
ΔS=∫V1​V2​​(∂T∂P​)V,N​dV=NkB​lnV1​V2​​.

For one mole with R=8.314Jmol−1K−1 and V2​=2V1​, this is ΔS=Rln2≃5.763JK−1. At 300K, a reversible isothermal expansion absorbs Q=TΔS≃1728.85J and performs equal work, since its internal energy is unchanged. The entropy difference is a state function difference: the same equilibrium endpoints give the same ΔS in an insulated free expansion, although there Q=0 and the process is irreversible.
The same Maxwell relations let thermal measurements determine the difference between constant-pressure and constant-volume heat capacities. In a smooth single thermodynamic phase,
dS=TCV​​dT+κT​α​dV=TCP​​dT−αVdP,
(43)
using heat capacity at constant volume, heat capacity at constant pressure, coefficient of thermal expansion and isothermal compressibility. Along fixed pressure, dV=αVdT, so
CP​−CV​=κT​TVα2​.
(44)
Thus measured expansion and compression responses determine a heat capacity difference without measuring both heat capacities separately. They do not determine the absolute heat capacities or absolute entropy by themselves; an independent thermal measurement supplies that missing information. For an ideal gas, α=1/T and κT​=1/P reduce the result to CP​−CV​=PV/T=NkB​, which is Mayer's relation.
When the necessary higher partial derivatives exist and commute, differentiating the Maxwell relations once more also gives
(∂V∂CV​​)T,N​=T(∂T2∂2P​)V,N​,(∂P∂CP​​)T,N​=−T(∂T2∂2V​)P,N​.
(45)
Integrating these slopes determines how a heat capacity changes with volume or pressure at fixed temperature. For an ideal gas, both right-hand sides vanish because the ideal gas law is linear in temperature at either fixed volume or fixed pressure. Consequently CV​ and CP​ depend only on temperature at fixed N, although they need not be constant in temperature. [ref]
Historically, James Clerk Maxwell's Theory of Heat, first published in 1871, presents these connections using the geometry of isothermal processes and reversible adiabatic processes. His fourth edition, page 167, explicitly relates expansion on heating at fixed pressure to heat emitted during an isothermal compression: the modern G relation gives δQrev​=TdS=−TαVdP. This explains why a substance with positive coefficient of thermal expansion emits heat when compressed isothermally, whereas one with negative coefficient absorbs it. [ref] [ref]

Diffusion (j=−D∇C)

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Diffusion is net transport associated with random microscopic motion. A localized patch of a dilute solute can spread through a stationary solvent: individual molecules move in both directions, but more cross from the crowded side of an imaginary surface than from the less crowded side. This imbalance gives a net diffusive flux down the concentration gradient; the molecules do not need to sense which direction has lower concentration. At uniform concentration, microscopic exchanges continue even though the net diffusive flux vanishes. [ref]
The distinction from advection is easiest to see in a dye patch. Uniform bulk motion carries its centre downstream; diffusion broadens it relative to that centre. Both can happen together. A moving or spreading patch by itself does not identify the mechanism: a nonuniform velocity field can also stretch a patch. [ref]
For a dilute nonreacting solute in a uniform medium at fixed temperature, Fick's first law models the relative diffusive flux as j=−D∇C, with scalar diffusion coefficient D>0 of units m2s−1. Here C is the amount of substance per unit volume, so j has units molm−2s−1. With carrier velocity field u, the total flux is Cu+j. The continuity equation, with no sources or chemical reactions, gives
∂t∂C​+∇⋅(Cu)=∇⋅(D∇C).
(46)
For constant D and incompressible flow, this reduces to Ct​+u⋅∇C=D∇2C, where ∇2 is the Laplacian. In a stationary carrier it is the diffusion equation. These assumptions matter: variable D must remain inside the divergence, and changing sources require extra terms. [ref]
The useful surprise is the common mathematics: thermal conduction smooths temperature through the analogous heat equation, while molecular diffusion smooths composition. This analogy already motivated the original formulation of Fick's laws. [ref] However, the thermal diffusivity and the solutal diffusivity need not be equal. A diffusive time scale tD​∼L2/D means that crossing ten times the distance requires roughly one hundred times the time. This is why molecular diffusion is especially effective across thin layers, and why chaotic advection can assist mixing by making those layers thinner. Physical diffusion is a transport mechanism, distinct from the broader probabilistic class of Markov diffusion.

Molecular diffusion

Words: 901
Diffusion OurBigBook.com
Molecular diffusion is the component of material transport caused by the random thermal motion of molecules, measured relative to bulk motion of their surroundings. A diffusion coefficient is a property of a particular substance in a particular medium under specified conditions, not a universal speed of spreading. Its dependence on the solute, solvent and temperature is precisely what makes a spreading experiment informative. A random walk idealizes this motion; the Brownian motion description provides a continuous approximation over sufficiently long times. [ref]
A motivating experiment: watch dye enter a gel. Samprovalaki, Robbins and Fryer studied rhodamine 6G and methylene blue entering agar gel from two side reservoirs. A covered slab, 10×5×1mm, sat on a controlled thermal stage; the dye was brought to the same temperature. They photographed the gel every ten minutes, averaged image intensity across a strip, and fitted the changing concentration to a diffusion equation model. The cover limited evaporation and stopped dye travelling over the gel surface. Runs at 30, 50 and 70∘C were repeated in triplicate. The measured spatial colour change therefore supplied a quantitative transport test, rather than merely showing that dye eventually spreads. Changing lighting also changes image intensity, so the optical response had to be checked. Importantly for interpretation, their constant-diffusion coefficient fit was imperfect and the gel coefficient is an effective transport coefficient, not automatically the value in free water. [ref]
A finite-pulse version to test width growth. The following is a proposed teaching variant, not that paper's apparatus or a report of measurements. Make a long, narrow, transparent gel channel of uniform cross-section. Join a thin dyed gel band between two undyed lengths of the same gel, with good contact and no air gaps; the dye should initially fill the cross-section so the dominant concentration variation is along the channel coordinate x. After assembly, keep the covered channel horizontal at uniform temperature, away from vibration. The dye is a finite initial pulse: no reservoir supplies more dye. Choose a dye whose image response can be calibrated and whose interaction with the gel is small enough for an approximately constant diffusion coefficient to be plausible.
Photograph the whole pulse at recorded times with fixed lighting, focus and exposure, including a length scale. Use uniformly dyed standards of the same gel thickness and a blank gel to convert image intensity to concentration C(x,t); do not assume raw brightness is proportional to concentration. Average across the channel width and examine several parallel strips to check the one-dimensional approximation. Measure the initial profile instead of treating the band as infinitely thin. For a finite pulse with negligible end effects, define its spatial integral Q, centre xˉ and width σ by
Q=∫−∞∞​C(x,t)dx,xˉ(t)=Q1​∫−∞∞​xC(x,t)dx,σ2(t)=Q1​∫−∞∞​(x−xˉ(t))2C(x,t)dx.
(47)
Here σ2 is the variance of the normalized profile C/Q, and σ is its standard deviation. If C is measured in molm−3, then Q has units molm−2; multiplying by the channel cross-section gives the total amount of substance. For the unbounded one-dimensional diffusion equation with constant D, conserved Q, finite variance and sufficiently decaying tails,
σ2(t)=σ02​+2Dt,D=21​dtdσ2​.
(48)
Thus plot width squared against time: its slope determines the diffusion coefficient, while its intercept includes the finite starting width. This moment law holds even for a non-Gaussian distribution initially; it follows by applying integration by parts twice to the diffusion equation. [ref]
For the particularly readable case of an initially Gaussian distribution centred at zero, uniform advection at speed u and constant diffusion coefficient D give the one-dimensional concentration profile
C(x,t)=2π(σ02​+2Dt)​Q​exp[−2(σ02​+2Dt)(x−ut)2​].
(49)
Its centre moves as xˉ=ut and its variance grows as σ02​+2Dt. Our illustrative choice σ0​=0.50mm and D=0.20mm2h−1 gives widths 0.50, 0.81 and 1.36mm at zero, one and four hours. These are calculated values, not a measured dye coefficient. Once 2Dt dominates the initial variance, width grows as 2Dt​: four times the elapsed time gives approximately twice the width. A rectangular starting band will not immediately have a Gaussian distribution, although the same width-squared law still applies under the stated assumptions.
Controls and limits of the interpretation. In the proposed experiment, check that Q stays constant and that the centre remains stationary while the width increases. Include a blank and a uniformly dyed gel photographed over the same period: an apparent signal change there exposes lighting drift, dye fading or evaporation. Repeat with a lower starting dye concentration and a second initial width; agreement of the slopes is a check on constant D and on preparation effects. Keep the pulse far from the channel ends and record its faint tails: truncation and background errors can strongly bias a variance. Poor contact, dye binding, chemical reactions or transport in a liquid film can invalidate the simple model. A gel suppresses bulk liquid motion, but its inferred diffusivity need not equal that in the pure solvent. A stationary centre alone does not exclude symmetric flows, and linear width-squared growth alone does not prove a molecular mechanism: turbulence can also produce an effective diffusive description. These are reasons to combine the profile test with the controlled setup.

Local detailed balance states that the logarithm of the probability ratio between a trajectory and its time reverse equals the entropy delivered to the environment in units of kB​. For one heat bath, log(PF​/PB​)=ΔQ/(kB​T) when positive ΔQ flows into the bath.

This is the path version of detailed balance. A time-even order parameter is read backward without changing sign, while a transport flux changes sign. The Onsager--Machlup path probability implements this reversal in a coarse-grained stochastic description.

Fluctuation theorem

A fluctuation theorem compares the probability of a fluctuating sample trajectory with that of its reverse. Consider a finite-duration Markov process with discrete, time-even states coupled to one thermal reservoir at positive temperature T. Let PF​[γ] include the initial probability ρ0​(x0​) of the sample trajectory γ. Define PR​ by reversing the control protocol and initializing it with the actual forward final probability distribution ρτ​. Write Θγ for the same states visited in reverse time order. Require normalized path laws with matching probability support: a path has positive forward weight exactly when its reverse has positive reverse weight. This excludes irreversible forbidden transitions and missing initial states.
Under local detailed balance, with positive heat Qbath​ delivered to the thermal reservoir, the full path-weight logarithm is
ΣF​[γ]=lnPR​[Θγ]PF​[γ]​=kB​TQbath​[γ]​+lnρτ​(xτ​)ρ0​(x0​)​=kB​ΔStot​[γ]​.

Define the conjugate reverse functional by ΣR​[η]=ln(PR​[η]/PF​[Θη]), so ΣR​[Θγ]=−ΣF​[γ]. Summing the path identity over paths with a given value gives the exact finite fluctuation theorem
pR​(−s)pF​(s)​=es,

for nonzero denominator, using probability masses or corresponding probability density functions. This ΣR​ is defined by the paired laws: it need not be the total entropy production obtained by independently restarting the thermodynamic construction for the reverse experiment. A generic driven experiment therefore does not imply pF​(s)/pF​(−s)=es.

A steady state does not by itself give every fluctuating observable an entropy production symmetry. If the dimensionless total entropy production Σt​ has the same-law finite relation and a large deviation principle with rate function I for Σt​/t, then, on its common domain,
pt​(Σt​/t≈s)≍e−tI(s),I(−s)−I(s)=s.

The first expression denotes leading exponential scaling; the second follows by taking the scaled logarithm of the probability ratio. A finite-state, autonomous Markov process with time-even states, positive bidirectional rates and a positive stationary distribution supplies a standard setting for a finite total-entropy production relation. The stochastic system entropy is then bounded, so its endpoint contribution does not change the long-time rate function of bath entropy production. [ref]
Unbounded state spaces can have endpoint fluctuations on the scale relevant to a large deviation principle. Dropping system entropy, changing the measured observable to heat, or changing the reverse preparation therefore requires a fresh argument. The exact finite integral fluctuation theorem, a same-law finite relation, and an asymptotic rate function symmetry are distinct claims.

Boltzmann distribution (Pi​=Z−1e−βEi​)

Words: 784 Articles: 4
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
The Boltzmann distribution assigns probabilities to individual microstates in a canonical ensemble, a statistical ensemble for thermal contact. The system exchanges energy with a thermal reservoir at fixed positive absolute temperature T, while its particle number N and external parameters, such as volume, stay fixed. The thermal reservoir is large enough that these exchanges barely change its temperature; the coupling permits thermal equilibrium but contributes negligible interaction energy. All the microstates considered have the same N. No chemical potential term is needed in their weights; fixed N does not imply that the chemical potential is zero.
For a finite discrete set of microstates with energies Ei​, write
pi​=Ze−βEi​​,β=kB​T1​,Z=∑i​e−βEi​,∑i​pi​=1.
(66)
Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, β is the inverse temperature, e−βEi​ is a Boltzmann factor, and Z is the partition function. The Boltzmann factor is a weight; dividing by the partition function makes it a probability. [ref]
The useful surprise is that a fixed temperature still permits thermal fluctuations in the system's energy. The Boltzmann distribution predicts their probabilities and expected values without tracking every microscopic exchange. Its exponential function also makes rare excited microstates sensitive to temperature: an energy gap much larger than kB​T gives strong Boltzmann suppression, while warming increases their relative populations. A population ratio can therefore reveal a gap or serve as a thermometer, provided thermal equilibrium and the relevant state degeneracies are known.
Historically, Josiah Willard Gibbs's Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902) presents the canonical ensemble in Chapter IV. His equations 90–92 give an exponential function of energy and its normalization, in classical phase space. This classical formulation exhibits the same weighting principle. [ref] [ref]

Statistical ensemble

Words: 55
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A statistical ensemble describes hypothetical copies of the same system under specified constraints, with a probability distribution over their microstates. An ensemble average is an expected value across those copies. The canonical ensemble fixes temperature and particle number while allowing energy exchange; the microcanonical ensemble fixes energy, and the grand canonical ensemble also allows particle exchange. These choices specify different physical preparations. [ref]

Temperature

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Temperature labels thermal equilibrium: two internally equilibrated bodies have the same temperature when contact permitting only heat exchange produces no net heat transfer. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the comparison transitive. If bodies A and B separately reach thermal equilibrium with the same thermometer without appreciably disturbing either body, they agree with each other. This is what lets a gas thermometer compare a metal block with water, despite their different internal energies and heat capacities. Insulation alone makes no such comparison: it can prevent heat transfer between bodies at different temperatures. [ref]
The zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes equality comparisons, but does not choose a numerical scale. Thermodynamic temperature supplies an absolute scale consistent with Carnot's theorem and entropy. For a simple compressible system at thermodynamic equilibrium with fixed particle number N and composition,
T=(∂S∂U​)V,N​,T1​=(∂U∂S​)V,N​.
(75)
Here U is internal energy, S is entropy, and V is volume; the second equality assumes the derivative can be inverted. Temperature is a thermodynamic conjugate variable to entropy and belongs to the intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities as an intensive quantity. Its partial derivative tells us how much internal energy must change per unit change of entropy under the stated constraints. More general systems require their other mechanical and material variables to be held fixed too. [ref]
For an infinitesimal quantity δQ>0 of heat transferred from A to B, with no work or matter exchange, the equilibrium entropy changes give
dStotal​=δQ(TB​1​−TA​1​).
(76)
For ordinary positive temperatures, spontaneous heat transfer from TA​>TB​ increases total entropy; thermal equilibrium has TA​=TB​. This comparison uses changes in entropy, rather than the total internal energy contained in either body. A small hot object can have less internal energy than a large cool one. See entropy maximization under thermal contact for the equilibrium criterion and negative temperature for the special case of bounded energy spectra.
Express absolute thermodynamic temperature T in kelvin, and a Celsius reading tC​ in degree Celsius:
∘CtC​​=KT​−273.15,∘CΔtC​​=KΔT​.
(77)
The offset is exact: 300K corresponds to 26.85∘C, and 400K to 126.85∘C. Their absolute temperature ratio is 4/3; dividing their Celsius readings gives a different number. Thus gas thermometer pressure ratios and Carnot's theorem require thermodynamic temperature. The modern SI definition of the kelvin fixes the Boltzmann constant kB​=1.380649×10−23JK−1; a reference bath realizes or transfers the scale rather than defining that constant.[ref]
Temperature is not universally the mean kinetic energy of a particle. In a classical, nonrelativistic ideal gas at thermal equilibrium, the equipartition theorem gives the mean translational kinetic energy relative to the gas's bulk motion:
⟨21​m∣v−u∣2⟩=23​kB​T.
(78)
Here m is particle mass, v its velocity, and u the mean flow velocity. In this regime, different particle masses at the same temperature have equal mean translational kinetic energies but different characteristic speeds. A moving gas can also carry bulk kinetic energy without being hotter in its rest frame. Internal molecular modes and quantum statistics require further care; the equipartition theorem has classical assumptions, whereas the equilibrium entropy definition applies more widely. [ref]

Thermometer

Words: 2k Articles: 5
Temperature OurBigBook.com
A thermometer measures temperature through a physical response whose relation to temperature is known. Examples include the length change from thermal expansion, a change in electrical resistance, and the pressure of a gas thermometer. If the response function X=f(T) is an injective function over the working range, its measured value determines T=f−1(X) through the inverse function. Thermometer calibration establishes that relation for the particular instrument and measurement conditions. Two matching readings are meaningful only after calibration to a common scale and with the probes sampling comparable equilibrium states. [ref]
For a contact thermometer, the sensing part must reach thermal equilibrium with the region being measured. That region may differ from the rest of the object: an immersed probe near a heater can read a local temperature while the surrounding water remains cooler. A stable reading can also be a steady state set by competing heat transfer paths to the sample and the room. Good contact, adequate immersion, mixing where appropriate, and checks for spatial differences help establish which temperature the reading represents. These are measurement controls inferred from the thermal equilibrium requirement, not a guarantee that every flat trace is equilibrium.
A thermometer also changes the sample it touches. Consider an original toy calculation with an initially uniform sample at To​=350K, a probe at Tp​=300K, and constant whole-body heat capacities Co​=100JK−1 and Cp​=1JK−1. Suppose together they form an isolated system, with no work or phase transition and negligible contact energy. The first law of thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium give
Tf​=Co​+Cp​Co​To​+Cp​Tp​​=349.50495…K,Tf​−To​=Co​+Cp​Cp​​(Tp​−To​).
(79)
The final thermometer reading underestimates the sample's original temperature by about 0.495K, although it correctly measures their new common temperature. The disturbance becomes small when the participating probe heat capacity is small compared with the sample's. A large controlled heat bath is a different limit: it supplies or removes heat while approximately maintaining its own temperature.
Waiting time is a separate issue from disturbance. Under a toy Newton's law of cooling model for a uniform probe in a maintained heat bath, a constant contact conductance G gives
Cp​dtdTp​​=G(Tb​−Tp​),Tp​(t)=Tb​+[Tp​(0)−Tb​]e−t/τ,τ=GCp​​.
(80)
The time constant τ controls this exponential decay. For stipulated values Tb​=350K, Tp​(0)=300K and τ=5s, the probe reads about 331.61K after one time constant and 347.51K after three. These are calculated values, not an instrument specification or measured data. Real probes may have multiple relaxation times and additional heat transfer paths; choose an equilibration criterion from the required accuracy, rather than assuming that a fixed waiting time works universally.

Here N is particle number, n is amount of substance, kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, and R is the molar gas constant. The reference and test states must be internally equilibrated, and T0​ must be known on the absolute thermodynamic temperature scale. A pressure ratio cancels the unknown gas inventory and bulb size in the ideal constant-volume limit. This cancellation is the method's appeal: a mechanical measurement transfers an absolute temperature scale between different materials. The Maxwell speed distribution and ideal gas pressure from wall collisions explain the microscopic origin of the response. [ref]
For an original ideal-model calculation, choose T0​=300K, P0​=120kPa and P=160kPa. Then T=400K. These are stipulated values, not observations. Both pressures must be absolute, referred to vacuum. If the surrounding atmospheric pressure were 100kPa, the corresponding gauge pressures would be 20 and 60kPa; their ratio is three, which would incorrectly predict 900K. A pressure difference from the atmosphere cannot be substituted into the ideal gas law.
A motivating calibration experiment. Schooley's account of the NBS/NIST work describes a helium-filled metal bulb, a capillary, a capacitance diaphragm gauge, and a mercury pressure standard. Circulating bath liquid passed the bulb assembly and platinum resistance thermometers. The resistance probes checked the surrounding temperature; gas pressure supplied the independent thermodynamic comparison. In an early series, workers filled the cleaned bulb with purified helium at the highest test temperature, checked pressure over three hours, then measured at lower temperatures and near a reference at 0∘C. Six filling pressures allowed extrapolation toward zero pressure. [ref]
To turn this principle into a readable measurement protocol, use the following controls. These steps are a proposed teaching interpretation of the cited apparatus, rather than additional reported NBS observations:
  • Define the inventory. Evacuate and clean the bulb and connecting tube, fill with a known pure gas, close the filling valve, and keep the same total particle number during each reference/test comparison. Monitor pressure at a maintained temperature before and after a run. A leak changes N; a slow drift can also reflect contamination, sorption, or imperfect equilibration, so pressure stability alone does not identify its cause.
  • Measure the reference. Place the bulb in a controlled environment with independently assigned T0​. Record P0​ after thermalization, together with the independent thermometer readings and their spread. A reference near 0∘C has an absolute temperature near 273.15K, rather than zero temperature. Repeating reference readings tests whether the inventory or apparatus changed during the comparison.
  • Measure the test state. Change the bath setting, allow the bulb and gas to settle, and record P only when the surrounding thermometers and pressure are sufficiently stable for the intended accuracy. Compare readings at different positions and vary the settling time. Record the connecting tube's temperature profile too: uniform bath temperature does not make the entire connecting tube isothermal.
  • Measure the volume changes. Determine the bulb's thermal expansion and its deformation from differences between inside and outside pressure. Measure the connecting tube's dimensions and the effective valve volume. “Constant volume” is the ideal model; a real vessel expands. These measurements supply corrections, even though the absolute bulb volume cancels in the simplest pressure ratio.
  • Measure pressure against a reference. For a liquid-column pressure standard, measure the vertical column height, the liquid's temperature-dependent mass density, local gravitational acceleration, and the reference-side pressure. Include diaphragm offsets and the gas's hydrostatic pressure change between the sensor and bulb. The pressure needed in the equation of state is at the bulb, not automatically at the remote gauge.
The corresponding NBS apparatus used a protective case with an outer helium layer held close to the bulb pressure, reducing pressure deformation while aiding thermal contact. Thermal expansion was measured on bulb material. Gas in the capillary remained partly outside the hot region, requiring a measured tube temperature profile and geometry. Pure working gas also mattered: contaminants that sorb on surfaces can change the freely circulating inventory. These are physical effects to measure or bound, rather than scatter that disappears by averaging. [ref]
For illustration, neglect connecting-tube gas and describe a uniform bulb with a dilute virial expansion in particle number density ρN​=N/V:
PV=NkB​T[1+B2​(T)ρN​+O(ρN2​)],T0​T​=P0​P​V(T0​)V(T)​Z(T)Z(T0​)​.
(82)
Here Z=PV/(NkB​T) and B2​ is the second virial coefficient in the particle-density convention; a molar-density convention rescales the coefficient. The second relation follows exactly from the definition of Z for the same N, and shows the signs of the corrections. If the bulb expands by 0.1% and Z=1 at both states, the toy pressure ratio above gives 400.4K, rather than 400K. Improved expansion and helium nonideality models really changed the temperatures inferred from the 1989 NIST data: Harvey's 2023 reanalysis found expansion updates of roughly 1–3mK and nonideality updates of roughly −0.1 to −0.5mK. Those are reported corrections to historical results, not the much larger illustrative correction just calculated. [ref]
With equal corrected bulb volumes, negligible or corrected connecting-tube gas, fixed reference and test temperatures, and a dilute classical single gas phase,
P0​P​=T0​T​[1+(B2​(T)−B2​(T0​))ρN​+O(ρN2​)],limρN​→0​P0​P​=T0​T​.
(83)
Repeat the reference/test comparison for several sealed fills, reducing N between comparisons but keeping it fixed within each pair. The extrapolation varies density at fixed endpoint temperatures; it does not cool one fill toward zero temperature. Real gases have different finite-density corrections but share the classical ideal gas intercept under these assumptions. The limit does not remove leaks, bulb expansion, gauge offsets, or the gas thermometer dead-space correction. At very low pressures, thermal transpiration can make remote sensor and bulb pressures differ through a nonisothermal capillary; this must be corrected too. The NBS work measured this pressure correction using a separate comparison of narrow and wider tubes. [ref]
At x=1, the toy models give Tapp​=407.92K and 388.12K, respectively, although their imposed true test temperature is the same. Their zero-density intercept is the reusable quantity. Measuring several low-density points permits a fit and a check for curvature; asserting a straight line from one finite-density point supplies neither. A practical fit must balance nonideality against increasing relative pressure error and the capillary corrections, and keep its extrapolation uncertainty.

Thermometer calibration compares an instrument's response with assigned reference temperatures under specified conditions. In a proposed two-reference procedure, thermalize the sensing part at T0​ and T1​, record responses X0​ and X1​, and, only if a linear response is justified over that interval, use
T(X)=T0​+(T1​−T0​)X1​−X0​X−X0​​.

Additional reference temperatures test curvature; returning to the first reference tests drift. A gas thermometer instead obtains its response from an equation of state, with a reference and corrections for its apparatus. In either case, uncertainty in the reference propagates to the inferred temperature. Calibration determines the response relation; it cannot by itself remove the finite-sample disturbance or incomplete thermal equilibrium described in thermometer. A reference established on a practical scale can also differ slightly from true thermodynamic temperature; the BIPM distinguishes the International Temperature Scale of 1990 readings from their thermodynamic counterparts.[ref]

Inverse temperature (β=1/(kB​T))

Temperature OurBigBook.com
Inverse temperature is β=1/(kB​T), where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature. A canonical ensemble weights an energy E by its Boltzmann factor e−βE. Calling couplings dimensionless means absorbing this factor β into their energy coefficients. The alternative convention kB​=1 makes inverse temperature 1/T; physical and dimensionless couplings must not be mixed.
In a thermal Euclidean worldline path integral with ℏ=1, β is also the circumference of the imaginary-time circle.

Thermal equilibrium

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Two internally equilibrated systems are in thermal equilibrium if bringing them into contact that permits only heat exchange causes no net heat transfer. In ordinary nonrelativistic thermodynamics without appreciable gravitational temperature shifts, their thermodynamic temperatures are equal. Merely preventing heat transfer with insulation does not establish thermal equilibrium: two insulated bodies can have different temperatures. [ref]
A thermometer illustrates the definition. Its own temperature settles to the object's temperature after thermal contact, provided its effect on the object is negligible. The existing zeroth law of thermodynamics makes this comparison transitive: two objects separately in thermal equilibrium with the same thermometer are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This lets one calibrated scale compare different materials.
Equal temperatures do not imply equal internal energies or equal heat capacities. Nor does thermal equilibrium by itself imply mechanical equilibrium or chemical equilibrium; these require additional allowed exchanges. There is also a distinction between no net exchange in thermal equilibrium and a constant temperature maintained by equal incoming and outgoing heat. The latter can be a steady state with ongoing entropy production. Microscopic exchanges can continue at thermal equilibrium, but their opposing contributions balance on average.
Historically, OpenStax credits the name “zeroth law” to Ralph Fowler in the 1930s: the already numbered laws needed a logically earlier statement about thermal equilibrium. [ref]

Assume each body remains internally uniform, their contact stores negligible energy, no phase transition occurs and no work is done or extracted. These are stipulated model values, not material measurements.
Because dUi​=Ci​dTi​, write Ui​=ai​+Ci​Ti​ with arbitrary fixed reference constants ai​. The conserved relative internal energy is
