Entropy (S)

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Entropy is an extensive quantity and a state function of an equilibrium system, measured in JK−1. Differences between equilibrium states are calculated along a reversible thermodynamic process:
S2​−S1​=∫12​TδQrev​​.
(99)
Here heat entering the system is positive and T is its absolute thermodynamic temperature. The reversible path used for calculation need not be the path actually taken. Dividing the actual heat by a single temperature generally fails for an irreversible process.
For example, put two rigid bodies, each with constant heat capacity C=100JK−1, at 600K and 300K in an otherwise isolated system. Assume each body has a uniform internal temperature, no phase transition occurs, and no work is extracted. Their final thermal equilibrium is at 450K, because the internal energy lost by one equals that gained by the other. Using entropy from heat capacity,
ΔSh​=Clog(450/600)=−28.77JK−1,ΔSc​=Clog(450/300)=40.55JK−1,
(100)
so ΔStot​=Clog(9/8)=11.78JK−1. One body's entropy decreases while the total increases. [ref]
In statistical mechanics, Boltzmann's entropy formula counts equally likely microstates compatible with a macrostate; Gibbs entropy handles a specified probability distribution over microstates. If the number of equally likely microstates doubles, entropy increases by kB​log2. The logarithm makes multiplicative counts additive for independent systems. These are precise statements about states and probabilities, not a universal measure of visible messiness. Calling entropy merely "disorder" obscures the thermal calculation above and hides which microstates are being counted. [ref]
The usefulness of entropy is that measurable heat capacities determine its changes, and the Second law of thermodynamics turns those changes into constraints on processes. It also connects macroscopic measurements to microscopic descriptions without requiring us to track every particle.

where p is pressure and ρ is mass density. Thus a homentropic flow has constant p/ργ.

Boltzmann's entropy formula (S=kB​logΩ)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Entropy OurBigBook.com
Why does a gas spread through an available container? One part of the answer is counting: a nearly uniform macrostate can be realized by vastly more microstates than a macrostate with every particle crowded into one corner. Boltzmann's entropy formula turns that multiplicity into entropy. The useful insight is that a large entropy measures how many microscopic realizations fit a specified macroscopic description, rather than how untidy a picture looks.
For a specified macrostate M containing Ω(M) accessible, equally likely microstates, write
S(M)=kB​lnΩ(M),pi​=Ω(M)1​(i compatible with M).
(102)
Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, and ln is the natural logarithm, also written log in this article's title. The count Ω(M) is dimensionless; entropy has units of energy divided by temperature. Always specify the macrostate, the constraints and the model's microscopic resolution before counting. A microcanonical ensemble provides a familiar equilibrium setting for the equal-probability assumption. [ref]
The natural logarithm compresses an enormous count into a manageable number and makes products of counts into sums of entropies; see additivity of Boltzmann entropy. With this counting convention, one allowed microstate has zero Boltzmann entropy. This zero refers to the chosen model and resolution; it does not by itself assign an absolute entropy to a real material.

Boltzmann entropy of a two-box occupancy (S(k)=kB​ln(kN​))

Boltzmann's entropy formula OurBigBook.com
Take N=20 distinguishable, labeled particles and two boxes of equal volume. Retain only whether each particle is in the left or right box: use a bit 0 for left and 1 for right. Each length-20 string is one coarse microstate of this toy model. Assume the labels make independent side choices with equal probability, so the 220=1048576 strings are equiprobable. Equal volumes motivate these weights for noninteracting particles with no preference for either box; equal volumes alone would not establish them for an arbitrary interacting gas.
Now retain only the number k in the left box as the macrostate. Choosing which k labels are left gives a binomial coefficient, so
Ω(k)=(k20​)=k!(20−k)!20!​,S(k)=kB​ln(k20​),P(k)=220(k20​)​.
(103)
The factorials count assignments to labels; the probability of a macrostate sums the probabilities of its constituent microstates. This is the binomial distribution with parameters 20 and 1/2. The same binomial coefficient appears in the counting of distinguishable two-level systems, although here the macrostate records occupancy rather than energy. [ref]
The largest binomial coefficient occurs at k=10, the balanced macrostate. All-left means k=20 and supplies just one string. Thus
Ω(10)Ω(20)P(10)​=184756,=1,≈0.176197,​S(10)/kB​S(20)/kB​P(20)​=ln184756≈12.126791,=0,=2−20≈9.53674×10−7.​
(104)
There are 184756 balanced strings for every all-left string, even though each individual string has the same probability. Exact balance has about 17.6% of the total probability; equilibrium reasoning concerns the many macrostates near balance too, rather than certainty of exactly ten particles on each side. The diagram compares the counts with their natural logarithms.
Four fair, independent coins give a smaller worked example with the same binomial distribution. If k is the number of heads, the five macrostates k=0,1,2,3,4 contain respectively 1,4,6,4,1 microstates. Their probabilities are respectively 1/16,4/16,6/16,4/16,1/16. In particular, two heads is one macrostate containing six ordered coin sequences, with Boltzmann entropy kB​ln6 in this counting analogy. A prescribed ordered sequence has one realization. The next diagram enumerates the same sixteen strings as left/right assignments.

In Boltzmann entropy of a two-box occupancy, impose an initial restriction that all labels are left. There is one allowed coarse microstate. Remove that restriction, allowing all occupancy values: the allowed set is now the union of every occupancy macrostate, containing 2N strings. If the final description assigns equal probability to this whole set, its Boltzmann entropy change is

This final description fixes neither box occupancy; it is coarser than the particular macrostate k=10, whose Boltzmann entropy is kB​ln184756. The two counts answer different questions, so substituting the balanced macrostate for the full allowed set would change the calculation.
For four labels, the initial all-left string is 0000; removing the restriction makes all sixteen strings available. The k=2 column has only six strings. Accordingly, the whole allowed set has Boltzmann entropy kB​ln16=4kB​ln2, while the balanced macrostate has Boltzmann entropy kB​ln6.
Removing a barrier changes the allowed set immediately, but it does not instantaneously randomize the actual probability distribution. Motion and equilibration must make those configurations accessible. The counting result illustrates the configurational contribution to free expansion; it does not describe the relaxation time or every contribution to the entropy of a real gas.

Additivity of Boltzmann entropy (ΩAB​=ΩA​ΩB​,SAB​=SA​+SB​)

Words: 133
Boltzmann's entropy formula OurBigBook.com
For two subsystems with independently specified macrostates, suppose every allowed microstate of A can be paired with every allowed microstate of B. Their allowed set is a Cartesian product. With equal probability for each pair, Boltzmann's entropy formula gives
ΩAB​=ΩA​ΩB​,SAB​=kB​ln(ΩA​ΩB​)=SA​+SB​.
(106)
For example, take two independent copies of the toy model, each with two labels choosing between its two boxes. Each copy has four configurations and Boltzmann entropy kB​ln4. Combining their independent labels gives sixteen configurations and Boltzmann entropy kB​ln16=2kB​ln4. This explains why entropy adds even though microscopic counts multiply. [ref]
The product assumption matters. A constraint shared between the subsystems can forbid some pairs; for example, fixing only their combined energy generally requires summing over its possible divisions. See entropy maximization under thermal contact for how thermal equilibrium selects the dominant division. Statistical independence cannot be inferred merely from drawing a boundary between two parts.

Scope of Boltzmann's entropy formula

Words: 293
Boltzmann's entropy formula OurBigBook.com
The strings in Boltzmann entropy of a two-box occupancy are complete microstates only within the binary toy model. They retain a coarse-grained variable for each particle and omit its exact position within a box and its momentum. An actual classical gas instead occupies continuous phase space; obtaining a dimensionless count from a phase space volume requires a specified cell convention and the appropriate treatment of particle identity. A quantum state count must respect the allowed quantum states and quantum statistics. Thus 2N is not a general count of microstates for a gas obeying quantum ideal-gas statistics. [ref]
For a discrete probability distribution with unequal weights, use the existing Gibbs entropy article; its equal-weight case gives Boltzmann's entropy formula. Shannon entropy uses the corresponding information measure, with the logarithm base setting its units. A count alone cannot replace the specified probability distribution, as the Boltzmann distribution examples demonstrate. [ref]
Overwhelming multiplicity explains why thermodynamic equilibrium is overwhelmingly probable in macroscopic systems under the appropriate statistical assumptions. It does not make low-entropy thermal fluctuations logically impossible. Nor does counting alone derive irreversible macroscopic evolution: one also needs dynamics, an initial preparation, and a reason the system samples the allowed microstates on the timescale of interest. [ref]
Historically, Boltzmann's 1877 paper counted microscopic arrangements, called complexions, and related the natural logarithm of their number to entropy. The Sharp and Matschinsky translation appeared in Entropy 17 (2015), pages 1971–2009, DOI 10.3390/e17041971. Its notation differs from ours: Boltzmann's permutability measure Ω is already logarithmic, whereas here Ω is the count. [ref] Josiah Willard Gibbs's Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902) developed the statistical ensemble framework; Chapter XIV compares several statistical definitions of entropy with thermodynamics. [ref] [ref]

Second law of thermodynamics

Words: 3k Articles: 14
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
For an isolated system, the second law requires ΔS≥0. More generally, include all affected surroundings to obtain
ΔStot​=ΔSsystem​+ΔSsurroundings​≥0.

Equality describes the reversible limit; irreversible macroscopic processes produce entropy. A closed system can lose entropy by exporting heat, so nondecrease does not apply to that system alone. The Clausius statement of the second law forbids a cyclic device whose sole effect is transferring heat from cold to hot. The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law forbids a cyclic device whose sole effect is converting heat from one thermal reservoir completely into work. Friction, free expansion and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference all introduce irreversibility. Moving arbitrarily slowly is insufficient if friction remains. Direct heat transfer in the opposite direction has positive total entropy change. A powered heat pump has a different budget: it supplies work and delivers more heat to the hot side than it extracts from the cold side.
A short equivalence argument links this restriction to the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law. Couple a hypothetical device that moves 600J from cold to hot with no other effect to the heat engine illustrated above, which absorbs 1000J, rejects 600J, and delivers 400J. The cold-side transfers cancel; the combined cyclic device takes 400J from the hot thermal reservoir and delivers exactly 400J of work, violating the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law. Likewise, a device discharging stored internal energy or consuming fuel has another effect. Converting supplied electrical work completely to heat through Joule heating reverses the proposed conversion and is allowed. The statement also allows cyclic devices that exchange heat with one thermal reservoir while consuming net work; it forbids positive net work output with that single heat source as the only external change.
Conversely, a hypothetical complete-conversion device could take 100J from the hot thermal reservoir and supply 100J of work to an ideal refrigerator that extracts 100J from the cold thermal reservoir and delivers 200J to the hot one. At 600K and 300K, that refrigerator is itself admissible: its reservoir entropy changes cancel. The composite would consume no external work and move a net 100J from cold to hot, violating the Clausius statement of the second law. Together with the construction there, this proves the equivalence of the two impossibility statements.[ref]

Let Qh​>0 be heat absorbed from the hot thermal reservoir and Qc​>0 the magnitude rejected to the cold one. Then

A short derivation now becomes transparent: the Second law of thermodynamics gives −Qh​/Th​+Qc​/Tc​≥0, and the first law of thermodynamics gives W=Qh​−Qc​. Together they yield the bound and, more precisely,
W=Qh​(1−Th​Tc​​)−Tc​ΔStot​.

As a computed contrast, the bodies with equal constant heat capacity in the entropy example would reach Tf​=600×300​=424.26K if a reversible engine extracted work until their temperatures matched. Zero total entropy change gives this geometric mean; the first law of thermodynamics then gives Wmax​=C(600+300−2Tf​)=5147.19J. Direct contact reaches 450K and extracts no work.
Carnot's 1824 book asked whether the useful output of machines driven by heat was fundamentally limited and whether changing the working substance could improve that limit. A Carnot cycle realizes the reversible bound in Carnot's theorem. Its four steps for an ideal gas working substance are:
  • Reversible isothermal expansion at Th​, absorbing Qh​ and increasing entropy by ΔS.
  • Reversible adiabatic expansion, doing work while the temperature falls from Th​ to Tc​ and entropy stays fixed.
  • Reversible isothermal compression at Tc​, rejecting Qc​ and decreasing entropy by ΔS.
  • Reversible adiabatic compression, requiring work to restore Th​ at fixed entropy.
The temperature versus entropy plot in the Carnot's theorem figure is therefore a rectangle traversed clockwise. Because δQrev​=TdS, its width is ΔS=Qh​/Th​. For the illustrated engine, ΔS=5/3JK−1: the upper step absorbs 600×5/3=1000J, the lower step rejects 300×5/3=500J, and the enclosed area is the 500J net work. Geometry displays the thermal efficiency without solving the gas motion. The two vertical steps are isentropic processes, not constant-temperature steps. [ref] [ref]
Reversible heat transfer is a limit of vanishing temperature differences; ordinary finite-rate transfer introduces entropy production. The Carnot cycle is a performance benchmark rather than a guarantee of useful power. Running it backward gives the ideal operation of a refrigerator or heat pump, with work supplied to move heat toward the hotter thermal reservoir. [ref]

An isothermal process changes a thermodynamic system while keeping its temperature constant. It need not keep its pressure, volume or internal energy constant, and it does not generally have zero heat transfer. An adiabatic process specifies zero heat transfer instead. For example, a slowly expanding ideal gas can absorb heat from a heat bath and deliver the same amount of work while its temperature stays fixed.
For a fixed amount of substance and composition, internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. With Q>0 for heat entering and Wby​>0 for work delivered to the surroundings, the first law of thermodynamics therefore gives
ΔU=Q−Wby​=0,Q=Wby​.
(115)
This equality does not determine either transfer until the path is specified. Isothermal ideal-gas work gives the reversible value; an insulated free expansion has a different value even when its equilibrium endpoints have the same temperature. The closed system convention here excludes changes in bulk kinetic energy and external potential energy.
A conducting cylinder in a large, stirred heat bath approximates an isothermal process when the piston moves slowly enough for thermal conduction to keep up. A quasistatic process keeps the gas close to internal thermodynamic equilibrium; a reversible thermodynamic process additionally requires negligible friction and vanishing driving differences in pressure and temperature. Exact equality of the gas and heat bath temperatures gives no finite heat transfer rate through a finite thermal resistance. The reversible description is a limit of arbitrarily small differences and arbitrarily slow motion, illustrated by the finite-rate isothermal piston model.[ref]
For a real gas, internal energy at constant temperature can change with volume because molecular interaction potential energy changes. In one smooth thermodynamic phase of a fixed-composition simple compressible system,
(∂V∂U​)T,n​=T(∂T∂p​)V,n​−p.
(116)
Thus an isothermal process generally has Q=ΔU+Wby​, with no reason to set ΔU=0. The right-hand side vanishes for the ideal gas law, but not generally for another equation of state.[ref]

Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Heat is energy transferred across a thermodynamic system's boundary because of a temperature difference. It is measured in joules, like work and internal energy. A hot cup transfers heat to cooler surroundings; its temperature describes its state, while the transferred heat describes a process. The cup stores internal energy, rather than a substance called heat. [ref]
For a closed system with unchanged bulk kinetic energy and potential energy, choose Q>0 for heat entering and W>0 for work done by the system. The first law of thermodynamics gives
ΔU=Q−W,dU=δQ−δW.
(123)
Here U is the stored internal energy. For example, a sealed piston cylinder receiving 20kJ of heat and delivering 5kJ of work gains 15kJ of internal energy. A closed system retains its matter while exchanging energy; it need not be an isolated system. [ref]
Unlike internal energy, heat is not a state function: different paths between the same equilibrium states can transfer different Q, with compensating differences in work. The symbol δQ records this dependence on the path; there is no stored quantity whose difference is always Q. The two paths in first law of thermodynamics illustrate this directly. Supplied heat can raise temperature as sensible heat, change a phase fraction through latent heat, or help supply expansion work. Measuring temperature alone therefore does not determine transferred heat.
For a reversible thermodynamic process, δQrev​=TdS, where T is absolute temperature and S is entropy. This identification requires reversibility: an irreversible adiabatic process has Q=0 and can nevertheless increase entropy. Likewise Q=ΔH, with enthalpy H, requires the particular fixed-pressure conditions in enthalpy. These distinctions make heat useful as a precise boundary-transfer quantity in heat engines, refrigerators and heating calculations.
Historically, James Prescott Joule's paddle experiments showed that stirring water with input work could raise its temperature, helping establish conservation of energy. The lesson is still useful: a temperature rise can result from work even without incoming heat. [ref]

Through a planar face of area A with uniform normal component q, the signed rate is Q˙​=Aq in W; positive q means heat travels in the chosen positive normal direction. Fourier's law determines the conductive contribution. In a bar with a constant cross-sectional area, steady thermal conduction without internal sources or side losses makes both q and Q˙​ constant along the bar. Constant Q˙​ need not mean constant q when the cross-sectional area varies.

Thermal conduction

Words: 3k Articles: 14
Heat OurBigBook.com
Thermal conduction transfers heat through microscopic interactions without bulk transport of matter. To predict the heating load through a bar, combine Fourier's law with conservation of energy and the imposed end temperatures. In the isotropic model with positive thermal conductivity k, the conductive heat flux points from high to low temperature, opposite to the temperature gradient. A spoon warming along its handle and heat escaping through a wall are familiar examples.
Consider a bar of length L=0.10m, constant cross-sectional area A=0.010m2 and constant thermal conductivity k=2Wm−1K−1. Maintain its ends at Th​=40∘C and Tc​=20∘C, with x increasing toward the colder end. Assume a steady state, one-dimensional thermal conduction, no internal sources and no heat transfer through the sides. The temperature falls by 20K over 0.10m, giving
dxdT​=−200Km−1,q=−kdxdT​=400Wm−2,Q˙​=Aq=4W.
(126)
The difference between the two readings in degree Celsius units is the same 20-kelvin difference. The positive heat flux carries heat toward increasing x.
The general solution under these assumptions is
T(x)=Th​−LTh​−Tc​​x,q=Lk(Th​−Tc​)​,Q˙​=LkA(Th​−Tc​)​.
(127)
A proof outline is enough to explain the straight line: conservation of energy in any small slice, with no accumulation, sources or side losses, gives dQ˙​/dx=0. Constant cross-sectional area gives dq/dx=0; constant thermal conductivity and Fourier's law then give d2T/dx2=0. Two integrations and the end boundary conditions determine the displayed affine function. This is why a visually simple temperature profile can encode a continuous flow of energy. [ref]
Doubling the length halves the rate, while doubling the cross-sectional area doubles it, at fixed end temperatures and thermal conductivity. This explains why a long narrow support can limit unwanted heat transfer, while a short broad path can help remove heat. Joining materials leads to thermal resistance in series. During initial warming, internal energy can accumulate and the temperature profile need not be a straight line; the time dependence is described by the heat equation and thermal diffusivity.
Now join two layers, each of length L1​=L2​=0.10m, with constant cross-sectional area A=0.010m2 and stipulated constant thermal conductivities k1​=1 and k2​=4Wm−1K−1. Keep the outer ends at 40 and 20∘C. Assume a steady state, one-dimensional thermal conduction, no internal sources or side losses, and perfect contact: the temperature is continuous at the interface, with no extra contact drop. For each layer, use the area-specific thermal resistance ri​=Li​/ki​ and Ri​=ri​/A. The series calculation gives
r1​+r2​=k1​L1​​+k2​L2​​=0.100+0.025=0.125m2KW−1,R1​+R2​=Ar1​+r2​​=12.5KW−1,q=0.125m2KW−120K​=160Wm−2,Q˙​=Aq=1.6W,ΔT1​=qr1​=16K,ΔT2​=qr2​=4K,Tinterface​=40∘C−16K=24∘C.​
(128)
The heat flux is continuous: otherwise energy would accumulate at the interface. Yet Fourier's law gives different temperature gradients, dT/dx=−q/k1​=−160Km−1 and dT/dx=−q/k2​=−40Km−1. Lower thermal conductivity requires a steeper temperature gradient to carry the same heat flux; equal lengths therefore give drops in the ratio 4:1. A kink in the temperature profile records the change of material while perfect contact keeps the temperature itself continuous.

This lets us size layered walls without solving a new differential equation for every layer. The structure matches Ohm's law: temperature difference plays the role of electric potential difference, the rate of heat transfer plays the role of electric current, and thermal resistance plays the role of electrical resistance. Fourier's law (q=−k∇T)

Words: 467 Articles: 2
Thermal conduction OurBigBook.com
Fourier's law predicts the local conductive heat flux from the local temperature gradient. In a continuum approximation with isotropic thermal conductivity k>0, its vector form and one-dimensional form are
q=−k∇T,q=−kdxdT​,Q˙​=Aqfor uniform normal flux over area A.
(130)
The heat flux q has units Wm−2, the temperature gradient has units Km−1 and the thermal conductivity has units Wm−1K−1. The rate of heat transfer Q˙​ has units W. These units distinguish a local material response from the total power crossing a surface.
The minus sign makes heat flow toward lower temperature: for k>0, q⋅∇T=−k∣∇T∣2≤0. In the worked bar in thermal conduction, dT/dx=−200Km−1 therefore gives q=+400Wm−2. Reversing the end temperatures reverses the heat flux. A zero temperature gradient gives zero conductive heat flux in this model.
Fourier's law is a constitutive relation expressing measured material behavior; it is not a consequence of conservation of energy alone. It applies locally and does not require a steady state. The straight-line bar solution additionally assumes constant thermal conductivity, constant cross-sectional area, no sources or side losses, and fixed end temperatures. Anisotropic materials require the directional response described by the thermal conductivity tensor. The scalar k used in the examples expresses the stated isotropy assumption. [ref]
Historically, Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur was published in 1822. In Chapter II, article 112, he writes the heat crossing a spherical surface as the product of thermal conductivity, elapsed time, surface area and the negative radial temperature gradient; article 113 balances the incoming and outgoing heat to obtain the heat equation for a sphere. The enduring idea is this connection between a local flow rule and a global prediction of changing temperature. [ref] [ref]
Thermal conductivity (k)
Words: 189 Articles: 1
Fourier's law OurBigBook.com
Thermal conductivity is the material response coefficient in Fourier's law. For an isotropic material it is a scalar k, with units Wm−1K−1; larger positive k means a larger conductive heat flux for the same temperature gradient. It can depend on temperature and composition. Direction-dependent response in an anisotropic material is described by a thermal conductivity tensor. The two worked examples use stipulated positive constants, rather than measured values for named materials.
Thermal conductivity describes material response, whereas thermal resistance also includes geometry: for the steady bar, Rth​=L/(kA). Doubling k at fixed length, cross-sectional area and end temperatures halves thermal resistance and doubles the rate of heat transfer. Doubling length changes thermal resistance without changing the material's thermal conductivity. This distinction lets a designer improve cooling either by choosing a higher thermal conductivity or by shortening and widening the path. It also explains why the less conductive layer in thermal resistance takes the greater temperature drop.
Thermal diffusivity answers a different question: how rapidly a temperature disturbance spreads. Its usual model κ=k/(ρcp​) also involves mass density ρ and specific heat capacity cp​, so equal thermal conductivities need not imply equal rates of warming.

Thermal diffusivity measures how rapidly thermal conduction smooths a temperature difference inside a material. Thermal conductivity measures the heat flux driven by a specified temperature gradient; thermal diffusivity also accounts for the heat capacity that must be warmed. A material can carry substantial heat yet change temperature slowly because it stores substantial internal energy per kelvin.
Write α=κ for thermal diffusivity, reserving k for thermal conductivity. In a homogeneous isotropic material,
α=ρck​=Cvol​k​,[α]=Jm−3K−1Wm−1K−1​=m2s−1.
(131)
Here ρ is mass density, c is specific heat capacity for the relevant mechanical constraint, and Cvol​=ρc is volumetric heat capacity. The familiar k/(ρcp​) uses specific heat capacity at constant pressure. For ordinary solids with negligible thermal expansion, the difference between the two constrained specific heat capacities is often neglected. A rigid fixed-volume model instead uses specific heat capacity at constant volume; a compressible moving fluid requires the accompanying work and transport terms. Thus the constraint is part of the approximation, not a choice made solely from the units. [ref]
Assume a stationary material in the continuum approximation, local thermal equilibration on times shorter than those resolved, no internal heating, no phase transition, and negligible convection and mechanical work. Combining conservation of energy with Fourier's law gives the one-dimensional balance
ρc∂t∂T​=−∂x∂q​=∂x∂​(k∂x∂T​).
(132)
If k,ρ,c are constant over the region and temperature excursion, this becomes the heat equation ∂t​T=α∂x2​T. If k varies, retain the differentiated product; replacing it with k∂x2​T loses a term. Anisotropic materials need a thermal conductivity tensor. The scalar constant-α examples below deliberately exclude these complications. [ref]
For an original comparison, stipulate two model materials with equal thermal conductivity k=2Wm−1K−1 and equal mass density ρ=1000kgm−3, but specific heat capacities cA​=1000 and cB​=4000Jkg−1K−1. Then
αA​=2×10−6m2s−1,αB​=5×10−7m2s−1.
(133)
At the same temperature gradient, both have the same instantaneous heat flux by Fourier's law. At the same initial temperature profile and boundary conditions, material B takes four times as long to smooth a given spatial pattern. With fixed end temperatures, identical geometry and no sources, both eventually have the same steady profile and heat flux. The larger heat capacity changes the transient, not this steady state. These are stipulated parameters, not measurements of named substances.

The thermal diffusion time tD​=L2/α, with α=κ the thermal diffusivity, is a characteristic scale for smoothing a temperature variation over length L. It is the thermal instance of the diffusive time scale. Rescaling x=Lx and t=(L2/α)t removes L and α from the constant-coefficient heat equation. Doubling length therefore multiplies comparable internal equilibration times by four; increasing thermal diffusivity by four divides them by four.
This scale is not a universal time of complete thermal equilibrium. A nonzero Fourier mode decays exponentially and never becomes exactly zero at finite time. The geometry, boundary conditions, initial pattern and accepted residual determine the numerical factor. For example, an insulated bar's slowest nonuniform Fourier mode has decay time L2/(π2α), and reducing its amplitude to a fraction ε requires
tε​=π2αL2​logε1​,0<ε<1.
(134)
External heat transfer can impose a longer cooling time even when internal temperature differences smooth quickly. Thermal diffusivity alone does not determine cooling to the room's temperature.

Laser flash analysis
Words: 481
Thermal diffusivity OurBigBook.com
Laser flash analysis measures thermal diffusivity by heating one face of a specimen briefly and recording the opposite face's temperature rise. The original 1961 experiment used a flash tube rather than a laser: a blackened thin metal specimen sat in an opaque ceramic holder, with thermocouple wires pressed against its rear face. An amplifier, oscilloscope and camera recorded the signal. Uniform front illumination and the black coating promoted uniform absorption; the opaque low-thermal conductivity holder blocked direct rear illumination and reduced edge losses. The delayed rear response reveals internal thermal conduction rather than direct heating of the sensor. [ref]
A modern version uses a laser or flash lamp, a specimen of measured thickness L, controlled initial temperature, and a rear-facing infrared detector with a synchronized recorder. The readout is a temperature rise versus time, starting from a pre-pulse baseline. Thermal conductivity additionally requires mass density and specific heat capacity; it is not obtained from timing alone. [ref]
Under ideal one-dimensional, insulated, constant-property assumptions, instantaneous uniform absorption in a very thin front layer gives the normalized rear rise
R(t)=T∞​−T0​T(L,t)−T0​​=1+2∑n=1∞​(−1)nexp(−L2n2π2αt​),t>0.
(136)
Here T0​ is the initial uniform temperature and T∞​ is the final uniform temperature in the insulated model. Fitting this curve estimates thermal diffusivity; each term has the same αKn2​ decay as the insulated-bar Fourier modes. Equivalently, the half-rise time t1/2​ solves R(t1/2​)=1/2. Writing s=αt/L2, the series gives s1/2​≈0.13879, hence
α≈0.13879t1/2​L2​.
(137)
This coefficient comes from the stated ideal heat equation solution, not from an empirical sensor calibration. It has been independently checked by solving the series equation. Absolute absorbed pulse energy cancels from the normalized curve; determining heat capacity from its absolute height needs additional information. [ref]
Parker and colleagues identify finite flash duration, heat loss, nonuniform illumination, recording bandwidth and electrical interference as practical limits. A specimen too thin responds during the pulse; one too thick allows losses before the rear rise finishes. They shielded the electrical chain and recorded a baseline; their reported tests were preliminary metal measurements near ambient and moderately elevated temperatures. [ref]
Useful additional controls are to measure thickness at several points, verify the recorder's time scale and detector response independently, record a no-pulse baseline, and repeat at different pulse energies while avoiding phase transitions. Compare different thicknesses of the same homogeneous material: ideal half-rise times scale as L2. Failure of these checks can expose finite-pulse effects, sensor delay, optical transmission, coating storage or edge losses; a thickness error is especially consequential because the inferred thermal diffusivity depends on L2. These are proposed diagnostic controls, not invented measurements. When the pulse is not short or the sample exchanges appreciable heat with its surroundings, fit a model that includes those effects instead of applying the ideal half-rise coefficient unchanged.

Heat capacity (CX​=(δQ/dT)X​)

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Heat OurBigBook.com
Heat capacity measures the heat supplied per small temperature increase along a specified process:
CX​=(dTδQ​)X​.
(138)
The subscript X records the constraint, such as fixed volume or fixed pressure. The units are JK−1. The symbol δQ emphasizes that heat is a transfer along a path, rather than a state function with a differential dQ. Consequently, an unspecified heat capacity does not determine the required heat.
For a closed system of fixed composition undergoing a quasistatic process, assume that only pressure-volume work occurs, with no friction and no change in bulk kinetic energy or potential energy. The first law of thermodynamics and H=U+pV, where U is internal energy and H is enthalpy, then give
δQ=dU+pdV=dH−Vdp,CV​=(∂T∂U​)V​,Cp​=(∂T∂H​)p​.
(139)
These partial derivatives define heat capacity at constant volume and heat capacity at constant pressure, with the amount and composition also held fixed. Integrating along the selected constraint gives Q=∫T1​T2​​CX​(T)dT within a single thermodynamic phase; Q=CX​ΔT requires constant CX​. [ref]
For a computed example, take a monatomic gas in the classical ideal gas regime, with amount of substance n=1mol and stipulated molar gas constant R=8.314Jmol−1K−1. The equipartition theorem gives U=3nRT/2, and the ideal gas law gives pV=nRT. Thus
CV​=23​nR=12.471JK−1,Cp​=25​nR=20.785JK−1.
(140)
For the same temperature increase ΔT=10K, the two processes require
QV​=124.71J,Qp​=207.85J,ΔUV​=ΔUp​=124.71J,WV​=0,Wp​=pΔV=nRΔT=83.14J.
(141)
Here work done by the gas is positive. At fixed pressure, the extra heat supplies expansion work; the internal energy increase is the same because internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. Their final volume values differ. [ref]
The practical value of heat capacity is that a measured heat input and temperature response can determine it. Once its constraint and temperature dependence are known, it predicts heating requirements and supplies entropy changes through entropy from heat capacity. [ref]

In the classical high-temperature limit, each independent harmonic oscillator contributes kB​ to the heat capacity at constant volume, where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. A three-dimensional crystalline solid with N chemical atoms has 3N vibrational normal modes in the bulk harmonic approximation. Its vibrational internal energy and heat capacity at constant volume therefore obey

Here U0​ is independent of temperature at fixed volume. Thus the Dulong-Petit law predicts CV​≃3NkB​ for a real solid in this regime. Per mole of chemical atoms, rather than per mole of a compound's formula units,

(147)
with molar gas constant R and Avogadro constant NA​. A formula unit containing r chemical atoms consequently has a classical vibrational prediction of 3rR per mole of formula units.
For example, in this ideal classical model, one mole of chemical atoms heated at fixed volume from 300 to 600K gains vibrational internal energy
ΔUvib​=3R(600−300)K≃7483.02J.

The heat capacity at constant volume stays the same even though the thermal part of the internal energy doubles. These temperatures illustrate the stipulated classical model; they do not assert that every real solid is classical at 300K.
The proof outline is the equipartition theorem: one classical harmonic oscillator has a quadratic kinetic energy and a quadratic potential energy, each with mean kB​T/2. Their sum is kB​T, whose derivative with respect to temperature is kB​. Summing over 3N normal modes gives 3NkB​. The classical result does not require equal angular frequencies: each harmonic normal mode contributes the same amount once it is classical. Overall rigid motions give only a finite-size correction to the bulk count. This independence from the individual angular frequencies makes the Dulong-Petit law useful as a quick estimate of a solid's heating requirement.
Experiments on freely expanding solids often measure the heat capacity at constant pressure CP​, whereas the harmonic prediction is for the heat capacity at constant volume CV​. In a smooth single thermodynamic phase of a simple compressible material, the difference between constant-pressure and constant-volume heat capacities is
CP​−CV​=κT​TVα2​,
(149)
where α=V−1(∂V/∂T)P​ is the volumetric coefficient of thermal expansion and κT​=−V−1(∂V/∂P)T​ is the isothermal compressibility. Using measured CP​ as an approximation to CV​ requires this correction to be small compared with CV​. [ref]
High temperature here means kB​T≫ℏω for the relevant vibrational normal modes, with reduced Planck constant ℏ and mode angular frequency ω. At low temperature, excitation across a quantum energy spacing is suppressed: modes with ℏω≫kB​T freeze out thermally, and the classical equipartition theorem fails. The Einstein model of a solid makes this loss of vibrational heat capacity explicit. The Dulong-Petit law is therefore an ideal high-temperature vibrational limit, not a statement that all solids have the same heat capacity at every temperature. Other contributions and departures from the harmonic approximation can matter even at high temperature. [ref]
Historically, Petit and Dulong's 1819 experiments compared the specific heat capacities of several elemental solids and found an approximately constant product with their relative atomic weights. Their original empirical regularity came before the classical harmonic explanation; it suggested that counting chemical atoms reveals a simpler pattern than comparing equal masses. [ref]

The Einstein model of a solid represents the vibrations of N chemical atoms by 3N independent one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillators, all with the same positive angular frequency ω. Equivalently, each chemical atom has three independent oscillator directions. The common angular frequency is a simplifying model assumption, not a claim about every vibration of a real solid. Hold the volume, N and ω fixed. Define the characteristic temperature θE​=ℏω/kB​ and the dimensionless ratio x=θE​/T. The vibrational internal energy is
U=3Nℏω[21​+ex−11​],x=kB​Tℏω​=TθE​​.
(150)
The first term is the zero-point energy 3Nℏω/2. It is constant at fixed ω, so it contributes no heat capacity at constant volume. The temperature-dependent term gives
3NkB​CV​​=(ex−1)2x2ex​=(1−e−x)2x2e−x​.
(151)
This is the vibrational heat capacity at constant volume of the model, with no expansion or other contributions included. [ref]
For a worked comparison, choose the model parameter θE​=300K. The normalized heat capacity at constant volume depends only on T/θE​:
T/θE​Temperature T in KCV​/(3NkB​)
0.1300.00454
0.51500.72406
13000.92067
26000.97942
At T=θE​, one mole of chemical atoms therefore has vibrational heat capacity at constant volume 3R(0.92067)≃22.965Jmol−1K−1, using the unrounded model value. Even at twice the characteristic temperature, the model remains about 2.06% below the Dulong-Petit law limit. These are calculations for the ideal Einstein solid, not material measurements.
A short derivation uses the thermal partition function of a quantum harmonic oscillator. The energy eigenvalues En​=ℏω(n+1/2) and their Boltzmann factors form a geometric series, giving the one-oscillator canonical partition function z=e−x/2/(1−e−x). The mean occupation is 1/(ex−1), hence the displayed U after summing over 3N independent quantum harmonic oscillators. Taking its derivative with dx/dT=−x/T gives the displayed heat capacity at constant volume. [ref]
The two limits explain the shape. At high temperature, a Taylor series in small x gives
3NkB​CV​​=1−12x2​+O(x4)⟶1(T≫θE​).
(152)
At low temperature, 1−e−x→1, so
3NkB​CV​​∼x2e−x⟶0(T≪θE​).
(153)
The zero-point energy remains even when the thermal response is tiny: freeze-out means that changing temperature scarcely changes the occupations, not that the chemical atoms have zero energy. This is the useful lesson of the Einstein model of a solid: the classical counting rule reappears when many levels are accessible, while discrete excitation spacings explain its failure upon cooling.
The exponential low-temperature decay is also the model's limitation. Real three-dimensional crystalline solids have acoustic phonon branches with arbitrarily small angular frequencies in the bulk limit. The Debye model includes these collective normal modes and predicts a low-temperature vibrational contribution CV​∝T3, which the single-frequency Einstein solid cannot reproduce. This qualification concerns the vibrational contribution; additional excitations can change a material's total heat capacity. [ref]
Einstein introduced the quantum treatment of solid vibrations in his 1907 paper Die Plancksche Theorie der Strahlung und die Theorie der spezifischen Wärme. Its historical importance is that quantum excitation energies explained why the classical Dulong-Petit law could fail; the modern quantum harmonic oscillator formulation above includes the zero-point energy explicitly. [ref]

Pressure measures the compressive normal force per unit surface area. For a uniformly loaded surface of surface area A, the magnitude of the perpendicular force is F⊥​=PA; locally, P=dF⊥​/dA. Its SI unit is the pascal, 1Pa=1Nm−2. A force parallel to the surface contributes shear stress, rather than pressure. In a gas, the steady macroscopic force comes from many microscopic transfers of momentum; ideal gas pressure from wall collisions makes this connection explicit. [ref]
For a computed example, a uniform pressure of 100kPa on a piston of surface area 10cm2=10−3m2 produces a perpendicular force of 100N. If the opposite face is exposed to 80kPa, the net force due to the two pressures is (100−80)×103×10−3=20N, directed toward the lower-pressure side. The pressure on either face and their difference answer different questions; gauge pressure records a difference from a specified reference, often atmospheric pressure.
A scalar pressure describes a gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium with isotropic random particle velocities: every wall orientation has the same normal force per unit surface area. Without this isotropy, normal stresses can depend on direction and a pressure tensor is needed. Thus random motion alone is insufficient; a preferred direction matters.
In thermodynamics, pressure and volume are thermodynamic conjugate variables. For a simple compressible system, reversible expansion delivers work δW=PdV, and at fixed entropy S and particle number N,
P=−(∂V∂U​)S,N​,
(154)
where U is internal energy. A large pressure therefore means both a large wall force per unit surface area and a large amount of expansion work per small increase in volume.

The Van der Waals equation is a simple real gas equation of state that can also describe a liquid-gas critical point. With particle count N fixed, write the volume per particle as v=V/N:
p=v−bkB​T​−v2a​,v>b,a>0,b>0,
(155)
or equivalently (p+aN2/V2)(V−Nb)=NkB​T. Here p is pressure, T is absolute temperature, and kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. In SI, v and b have units m3 per particle, a has units Pam6=Jm3, and kB​ has units JK−1; the particle count is dimensionless. The pole at v=b excludes smaller volume values from this model.
The b correction represents excluded volume; the attraction term lowers pressure at fixed temperature and particle number density 1/v. This is a mean-field theory, replacing detailed intermolecular structure by two parameters. At v≫b with a/v2≪kB​T/v, it approaches the ideal gas law pv=kB​T. It supplies a useful qualitative route from a dilute gas to phase coexistence, without a claim of quantitative accuracy for every fluid.[ref]
Do not mix this particle convention with the molar volume convention elsewhere in this article. With amount of substance nmol​=N/NA​, Avogadro constant NA​, and molar gas constant R=NA​kB​, one has vm​=NA​v, bm​=NA​b, and am​=NA2​a, so p=RT/(vm​−bm​)−am​/vm2​. The molar parameters have units m3mol−1 and Pam6mol−2, respectively.
Johannes Diderik van der Waals introduced this equation of state in 1873, connecting molecular attraction with departures from the dilute ideal gas law. Its historical significance is the unified treatment of gases and liquids, rather than a universally exact fit.[ref]

Andrews's carbon dioxide experiment

Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The 1869 The Bakerian Lecture: On the Continuity of the Gaseous and Liquid States of Matter by Thomas Andrews describes dried carbon dioxide trapped above mercury in a sealed capillary tube. A steel screw pressurized water in a strong copper tube; movable mercury transmitted the load. A second capillary tube held air as a pressure gauge. Flowing water around the visible capillary tubes controlled temperature; a thermometer read the bath. A cathetometer read column positions, converted to volume readings using weighed-mercury calibration.[ref]
Below the critical temperature, compression produced a visible liquid–gas boundary; above it, large density changes occurred without that boundary. Three trials gave 30.92∘C as his critical temperature. Purity checks detected residual air; mercury height corrections accounted for unequal hydrostatic pressures. He explicitly left air nonideality and pressure-induced tube-capacity corrections unresolved, so his air-gauge pressures were approximate. These readouts support a liquid-gas critical point; they do not measure a homogeneous unstable loop or establish universal quantitative accuracy of the later Van der Waals equation.[ref]

Internal energy (U)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Internal energy U is the energy stored in the microscopic degrees of freedom of a thermodynamic system: random molecular kinetic energy, internal molecular excitations, and interaction potential energy. Its value requires a specified system and an energy reference. In thermodynamic equilibrium, internal energy is a state function; it records the present state, without remembering whether a previous change came from stirring, compression or heat transfer. This makes internal energy the common accounting quantity connecting mechanical experiments to thermal ones.[ref]
Heat and work describe energy crossing the system boundary during a process. They are not separately stored contents of the system. For a closed system whose bulk kinetic energy and external potential energy have unchanged endpoint values, the first law of thermodynamics gives
ΔU=Qin​+Won​=Qin​−Wout​.
(168)
Here Qin​ is positive for incoming heat, and Won​=−Wout​ is positive for net work done on the system. Two routes between the same equilibrium states have the same ΔU, although their heat and work can differ. The infinitesimal notation dU=δQin​+δWon​ distinguishes a state function change from path-dependent transfers.[ref]
For a calculated example, take one mole of a classical monatomic gas in the ideal gas regime, at fixed volume, from 300 to 310K. With stipulated molar gas constant R=8.314Jmol−1K−1, its internal energy change is 3nRΔT/2=124.71J. A purely thermal route supplies Qin​=124.71J with Won​=0. An ideal insulated stirring route supplies Won​=124.71J with Qin​=0, measured between equilibrium endpoints after the motion dies away. The same stored increment has two different transfer histories; neither history defines a separate kind of stored energy.
The familiar internal energy of an ideal gas is a useful special case. Neglect intermolecular interactions, hold the amount of substance n and composition fixed, and suppose that f independent quadratic terms per particle obey the classical equipartition theorem. Choosing the constant reference contribution as zero gives
U=2f​nRT,CV​=2f​nR.
(169)
Here T is absolute temperature, R is the molar gas constant, and CV​ is the whole sample's heat capacity at constant volume. A monatomic gas has f=3 translational terms. A rigid diatomic molecule has f=5 when its two rotational terms are active and vibration is frozen; activating one harmonic oscillator vibration adds two terms, one kinetic energy and one potential energy, giving f=7. The counting is of quadratic contributions, so a vibrational coordinate is not just one contribution.[ref]
This constant-f formula applies only over a regime with those same active terms, classical translational statistics, nonrelativistic motion and unchanged composition. Quantum freezing, quantum degeneracy, chemical reactions or appreciable intermolecular interactions invalidate that simple counting. More generally, at fixed amount and composition an ideal gas can still have U=U(T) with varying heat capacity at constant volume, so use ΔU=∫T1​T2​​CV​(T)dT. A nonzero constant reference adds U∗​ to fnRT/2 without altering ΔU.

Internal energy and system boundaries

Internal energy OurBigBook.com
For an ordinary stationary laboratory sample, a useful convention is
Etotal​=U+Kbulk​+Φext​,ΔU+ΔKbulk​+ΔΦext​=Qin​+Won​.
(170)
The bulk kinetic energy Kbulk​ includes organized whole-body motion; for pure translation it is Mvcm2​/2, with total mass M and center of mass speed vcm​. The external potential energy Φext​ includes elevation in an imposed gravitational field, approximately Mgz in a uniform field. Accelerating a sealed bottle or lifting it without otherwise changing its state changes these mechanical terms, rather than its internal energy. Molecular kinetic energy is measured relative to the chosen bulk motion.[ref]
State the convention rather than applying this separation blindly. If an experiment separately tracks a rotating apparatus or an organized flow, its mechanical kinetic energy must not also be counted in U. In Joule's paddle-wheel experiment, waiting for the apparatus and fluid to come to rest removes such an endpoint ambiguity. Including the vessel and paddle changes whose internal energy is measured; including the falling weights additionally puts their changing gravitational potential energy inside the enlarged system's total energy balance.

Internal energy OurBigBook.com
Constant temperature does not generally mean constant internal energy. At fixed amount and composition, within one smooth thermodynamic phase of a simple compressible system, an equilibrium identity is
dU=CV​dT+[T(∂T∂p​)V​−p]dV.
(171)
The bracket vanishes for the ideal gas law pV=nRT. It need not vanish for a real gas: changing the volume changes the average interaction potential energy, even when the random-motion contribution stays at the same temperature. The identity follows by writing dU=TdS−pdV and using a Maxwell relation; it does not require the actual process to be reversible. [ref]
For a Van der Waals equation model with volume per mole v=V/n, p=RT/(v−b)−a/v2 gives (∂U/∂V)T,n​=a/v2. Thus an isothermal expansion from v1​ to v2​>v1​, at fixed amount of substance n, increases internal energy by
ΔU=na(v1​1​−v2​1​)>0.
(172)
Separating attractive particles makes their interaction potential energy less negative. For stipulated n=1mol, a=0.10Pam6mol−2, b=10−5m3mol−1, T=300K, v1​=0.010 and v2​=0.020m3mol−1, the calculated increase for this one-mole sample is 5J, despite ΔT=0. This dilute stable-branch model example is not a measurement of a named gas. [ref]
A phase transition gives another reason. During equilibrium vaporization of a pure substance at fixed pressure, the temperature can stay at its phase coexistence value while the phase fraction changes. Molecular separation changes interaction potential energy.[ref] If the closed system does only pressure-volume work, its latent heat input obeys
Qin​=ΔH,ΔU=ΔH−pΔV.
(173)
Here H=U+pV is enthalpy. A vaporization latent heat therefore is not automatically the internal energy increment: some input supplies expansion work. A fixed temperature reading alone cannot tell how much internal energy changed.

Joule's paddle-wheel experiment

Words: 547 Articles: 1
Internal energy OurBigBook.com
Joule's paper On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat (1850) describes a copper vessel holding water and a brass paddle with stationary vanes. Descending lead weights drove its shaft through strings and pulleys; the vanes opposed simple co-rotation. A boxwood shaft segment reduced thermal conduction. He measured fall distances and initial/final temperatures, repeating twenty descents per run and disconnecting the drive for rewinding. Calibrated thermometers read the water and room.[ref]
His matched resting trials retained the water amount, duration, surroundings and reading procedure, omitting paddle motion to estimate environmental heat exchange. A screen reduced thermal radiation from his body. His calculation included the vessel and paddle heat capacities, external pulley/string losses, descent kinetic energy and string elasticity; it acknowledged residual vibration and sound.[ref]
The measured observable is a corrected temperature rise, interpreted through the participating heat capacity; it is not a direct view of molecular motion. The experiment tests whether measured mechanical input accounts quantitatively for thermal storage. Frictional warming by itself would establish neither the conversion factor nor the absence of heat exchange. A modern authored demonstration at UCSB instead measures crank turns and a cylinder's temperature with an electrical thermometer: the apparatus differs, but again both mechanical input and thermal response must be measured. [ref]

Paddle-wheel calorimetry energy balance

Choose the water, vessel and immersed paddle as the closed system, with fixed outer volume and negligible endpoint changes in bulk mechanical energy. Between common equilibrium temperatures T1​ and T2​,
ΔUassembly​=∫T1​T2​​Ceff​(T)dT=Wshaft,on​+Qroom,in​.
(174)
The effective heat capacity Ceff​ includes every component that participates in the common temperature change. For nearly constant Ceff​, the readout is Ceff​ΔT. Heat transferred between water and paddle stays inside this boundary; it must not be added again as external input. The drive supplies shaft work even though the vessel has no expansion work.
For a simplified modern model, let M be the total descending mass, let each of N descents cover height h, and let Wloss,out​ be energy diverted by the external drive. With negligible remaining drive kinetic energy and elastic storage,
Wshaft,on​=NMgh−Wloss,out​,NMgh=Ceff​ΔT+Wloss,out​+Qroom,out​.
(175)
The signed Qroom,out​=−Qroom,in​ may be negative if the room warms the assembly. This model omits the small endpoint and elastic corrections explicitly considered in the historical analysis. It does not equate all of the weights' lost gravitational potential energy with the water's gained internal energy.
As a proposed modern protocol, measure the falling masses and distances, calibrate the thermometer and Ceff​ independently, record room temperature and resting drift before and after each run, and wait for fluid motion to decay before the final equilibrium reading. Repeat with different fall budgets and run durations. A stable ratio of corrected input to corrected thermal storage supports the first law of thermodynamics over the tested range. Resting controls only estimate leakage if their thermal conditions represent the driven run; sensor lag, nonuniform temperature, unmeasured drive losses, evaporation or changing heat capacity can spoil the inference. Those are limits of the measurement, rather than evidence that heat was stored as a separate substance.

A free energy is a thermodynamic potential that compares possible states under specified environmental constraints. For a closed system of fixed composition, treated as a simple compressible system with only pressure-volume work, stable thermodynamic equilibrium minimizes Helmholtz free energy at fixed temperature and volume, or Gibbs free energy at fixed temperature and pressure. The choice follows the experiment: a rigid sealed vessel and a sealed cylinder with a freely moving loaded piston impose different constraints. Both may exchange heat with a thermal reservoir. See W. C. Carter, MIT thermodynamics notes, sections 2-1.14 and 2-1.19.
The useful insight is that internal energy alone cannot rank these alternatives: exchanging heat also changes the surroundings' entropy. Subtracting TS packages that accounting into a property of the chosen system. Adding pV additionally accounts for displacing the surroundings at fixed pressure. A free energy is a state function; supplied heat describes a transfer during a process. Under the stated constraints, supplied heat is Q=ΔU at fixed volume or Q=ΔH at fixed pressure, whereas neither ΔF nor ΔG generally equals Q.
A lower free energy identifies a thermodynamic preference, without specifying a timescale. A barrier can trap a system in a local minimum, producing metastability although a lower global minimum exists. The enzyme example illustrates the corresponding distinction for chemical reactions: changing the route can change the reaction rate while preserving the endpoint Gibbs free energy difference and chemical equilibrium.

Helmholtz free energy (F)

Words: 273
Thermodynamic free energy OurBigBook.com
The Helmholtz free energy is
F=U−TS,
(176)
where U is internal energy, also denoted E elsewhere here, T is absolute temperature, and S is entropy. For the closed system of fixed composition and only pressure-volume work described above, spontaneous relaxation at fixed temperature and volume cannot increase F. Stable thermodynamic equilibrium is a global minimum over the permitted alternatives, including different thermodynamic phases. A rigid vessel fixes the total volume; it does not require each coexisting thermodynamic phase to retain its own volume.
For a constructed comparison at 300K, suppose one candidate has 1.5kJ more internal energy but 6JK−1 more entropy than another at the same temperature and volume. Its difference is
ΔF=1500−300(6)=−300J.
(177)
Thus the candidate with higher internal energy has lower Helmholtz free energy. This is the practical reason for retaining the entropy term when selecting a state.
For equilibrium states within a smooth branch of fixed composition, the first law of thermodynamics gives dU=TdS−pdV, hence
dF=−SdT−pdV,S=−(∂T∂F​)V​,p=−(∂V∂F​)T​.
(178)
These derivatives extract entropy and pressure; the differential is not an evolution equation for relaxation. If chemical species amounts ni​ vary, add ∑i​μi​dni​, with molar chemical potentials μi​. A closed system can still change chemical species amounts through chemical reactions; the fixed-composition simplification then needs the conserved-inventory constraints of chemical equilibrium. See MIT 5.60, Lecture 14, fundamental equations and chemical potentials.
The minimum principle has a short explanation. At fixed volume, no boundary work occurs, so Q=ΔU. A thermal reservoir at positive temperature T loses entropy Q/T. Consequently
ΔStotal​=ΔS−TΔU​=−TΔF​≥0,
(179)
by the Second law of thermodynamics. Here both endpoint states share the imposed temperature. See MIT 5.60, Lecture 12, criteria for spontaneous change.
The microscopic counterpart is F=−kB​TlnZ in the canonical ensemble, with Boltzmann constant kB​ and partition function Z. The partition function examples compute the balance between internal energy and entropy; the chemical equilibrium example already displays an ideal-mixture Helmholtz free energy minimum.

Thermodynamic free energy OurBigBook.com
The Gibbs free energy is
G=U−TS+pV=H−TS,H=U+pV,
(180)
where H is enthalpy. For a closed system of fixed composition, with only pressure-volume work, spontaneous relaxation at fixed temperature and pressure cannot increase G; stable thermodynamic equilibrium minimizes it over the allowed states. A loaded piston can move while maintaining the imposed pressure, so the enthalpy term includes the displacement cost. Along a smooth equilibrium branch of fixed composition,
dG=−SdT+Vdp.
(181)
Thus its temperature slope at fixed pressure is −S, while its pressure slope at fixed temperature is V. See MIT 5.60, Lecture 13, Gibbs free energy and its derivatives.
Consider two illustrative thermodynamic phases, A and B, of the same substance at one fixed pressure. Write B minus A, using quantities per mole:
ΔH=12kJmol−1,ΔS=40Jmol−1K−1=0.040kJmol−1K−1.
(182)
Treat these differences as approximately constant over a limited temperature window. Then
kJmol−1ΔG(T)​=12−0.040KT​,T∗​=ΔSΔH​=300K.

At 280K, ΔG=+0.8kJmol−1, so A is preferred. At 320K, ΔG=−0.8kJmol−1, so B is preferred. At 300K, both have equal molar Gibbs free energy, permitting phase coexistence in this bulk model. B's greater entropy outweighs its greater enthalpy above the crossing.
Each plotted point compares alternatives at the same temperature; moving along the curve changes the imposed temperature. The model predicts preference, not instantaneous conversion: nucleation barriers can sustain metastability. Real enthalpy and entropy differences generally vary with temperature through heat capacities, bending this line outside the approximation.
At fixed pressure, the first law of thermodynamics gives Q=ΔH under the stated work restriction, so the same thermal reservoir accounting yields ΔStotal​=−ΔG/T≥0. Variable composition restores ∑i​μi​dni​ to dG; constrained Gibbs minimization for chemical equilibrium handles those permitted changes.
The historical foundation is Gibbs's [ref]. Its equations (87) and (91) introduce the combinations now called Helmholtz free energy and Gibbs free energy, connecting entropy criteria, chemical potentials and phase coexistence within one framework.

Identifying this enthalpy difference with supplied heat assumes a closed system and an equilibrium conversion with only pressure-volume work. [ref]

For a constructed fixed-pressure model, take m=1kg, initial temperature 280K, transition temperature Ttr​=300K, solid specific heat capacity at constant pressure cs​=2kJkg−1K−1, latent heat L=100kJkg−1, and liquid specific heat capacity at constant pressure cl​=3kJkg−1K−1. Heating the solid to 300K takes 40kJ of sensible heat; converting it fully to liquid takes another 100kJ of heat; heating the liquid to 320K takes 60kJ. The total is 200kJ. After a total heat input of 90kJ, x=(90−40)/100=1/2 and the temperature is still 300K. The corresponding per-unit-mass entropy jump is L/Ttr​=31​kJkg−1K−1.

Its heat capacity can have a jump or a singularity without a finite interval in which added heat converts coexisting thermodynamic phases at a constant temperature. The Clapeyron equation connects the slope of a phase coexistence curve to the latent heat and the change in volume during a first-order phase transition. A steep boundary can indicate a large latent heat, a small change in volume, or both. This lets a measured boundary constrain caloric properties and predicts how changing pressure shifts a melting temperature.
For a pure substance in bulk phase coexistence, label the initial and final thermodynamic phases α and β. Both have the same absolute temperature T, pressure p, and chemical potential. With s, h, and v denoting entropy, enthalpy, and volume on one common basis, define Δs=sβ​−sα​, Δh=hβ​−hα​, and Δv=vβ​−vα​. Then
dTdp​=ΔvΔs​=TΔvL​​,L=Δh=TΔs.
(190)
The derivative follows the phase coexistence curve; it is not a partial derivative within one thermodynamic phase. Use molar volume vm​ with molar latent heat Lm​ in Jmol−1, or specific volume v with latent heat L in Jkg−1. Both give dp/dT in PaK−1. For molar mass M, Lm​=ML and Δvm​=MΔv, so the predicted slope is independent of the chosen basis. This formulation assumes a simple compressible system, fixed composition, and negligible interface contributions; a curved interface can instead require the Young–Laplace equation.
For positive latent heat in the stated conversion direction, the sign of the slope is the sign of Δv. Converting liquid to gas normally increases volume and gives a positive slope. The negative melting-point slope of water illustrates the opposite sign. At a thermodynamic critical point, the coexisting gas and liquid merge: both L and Δv vanish, so their ratio needs a limiting analysis rather than substitution of zero into the Clapeyron equation.[ref]
A short derivation uses the molar Gibbs free energy gm​, equal to the chemical potential for a pure substance. Equality persists along the boundary, so dgm,α​=dgm,β​ with dgm​=−sm​dT+vm​dp. Therefore −Δsm​dT+Δvm​dp=0. Equality of gm​=hm​−Tsm​ also gives Δhm​=TΔsm​. Eliminating Δsm​ yields the Clapeyron equation.

A concrete experiment turns the phase coexistence curve into pairs of temperature and saturation pressure. A 1969 paper reports water measurements made in 1942 and 1947–1949 using a boiler and precision mercury manometer. Platinum resistance thermometers read the boiler temperature through a resistance bridge. The pressure-transfer line passed through an ice-water condenser and a dry-ice trap; helium filled connecting sections. Corrected mercury column height gave the pressure at the thermometer coils, including hydrostatic pressure contributions from water vapor, helium, mercury, and mercury vapor.[ref]
Controls included normal/reversed-lead readings, readings at two thermometer electric currents extrapolated to zero current to remove self-heating, repeated bridge calibration, and daily triple point thermometer calibration checks. Cellar temperature measurements corrected fluid-column and gauge-block thermal expansion. One measurement series was excluded because a trapped gas bubble was suspected of corrupting the mercury head. The paper adjusted measurements to round temperatures using previously tabulated slopes; those adjusted values therefore are not independent measurements of those slopes.[ref]

Leaks, contamination, or a temperature gradient can spoil that interpretation. Converting a measured phase coexistence curve slope directly into latent heat instead assumes that equation; it is not an independent test.

The chemical potential measures how a thermodynamic potential changes when matter is added under specified constraints. It plays for matter exchange the role that temperature plays for heat exchange: a difference supplies a direction, and equality characterizes thermodynamic equilibrium when the corresponding exchange is allowed. This connects diffusion, phase coexistence and chemical equilibrium through one quantity.
For a single component, the particle convention is
μparticle​=(∂N∂U​)S,V​,
(199)
where U is internal energy, N counts particles, S is entropy and V is volume. This partial derivative holds entropy and volume fixed; it measures an incremental change rather than the average energy per particle. See David Tong, Statistical Physics, section 1.4.
In chemistry the molar convention instead uses amount of substance n, measured in moles:
μm​=(∂n∂G​)T,p​,n=NA​N​,μm​=NA​μparticle​.
(200)
Here G is Gibbs free energy, T is temperature, p is pressure and NA​ is the Avogadro constant. The units are J per particle versus Jmol−1. For several chemical species, define each chemical potential by varying only its own particle count or amount of substance, with all other components' counts or amounts fixed. Many texts use μ for either convention, so the units and the variable being differentiated must identify it.
For a simple compressible system with variable component inventories, the fundamental differentials are
dU=TdS−pdV+∑i​μparticle,i​dNi​,dG=−SdT+Vdp+∑i​μm,i​dni​.
(201)
They describe changes between states in thermodynamic equilibrium with only pressure-volume work. If every component inventory is fixed, the sums vanish. The Gibbs free energy form follows by differentiating G=U−TS+pV and using dNi​=NA​dni​; this is why the two definitions describe the same chemical potential in different units.
A chemical potential can be negative. Holding entropy fixed while adding matter need not increase internal energy; Tong explains this explicitly for a classical ideal gas in Statistical Physics, section 2.2.4. Its absolute sign also depends on the reference energy: replacing U by U+ϵ0​N shifts μparticle​ by ϵ0​. A common reference shift cancels from differences for the same chemical species, which are what determine exchange. Thus “energy cost” means a signed increment, not an always positive amount that must be supplied.

Hence exchange toward lower chemical potential lowers Gibbs free energy. If transfer is allowed in both directions and the two reservoirs contain the exchangeable component, thermodynamic equilibrium requires equal chemical potentials for that component. See MIT 5.60, Lecture 14, pages 1–2.
An impermeable partition can maintain unequal chemical potentials; equality is a condition on an allowed exchange. Two pure samples of the same ideal gas already have equal chemical potentials at the same temperature and pressure. Different compositions at a common pressure can instead give different chemical potentials for one component through its thermodynamic activity.
Equality concerns the same exchangeable component in different places, not all different chemical species. For a permitted chemical reaction, the corresponding interior chemical equilibrium criterion is ∑i​νi​μm,i​=0, with signed stoichiometric vector entries νi​. The existing chemical equilibrium and constrained Gibbs minimization for chemical equilibrium sections develop those composition constraints.

Rigid compartments impose a different constraint: fixed volume rather than fixed pressure. With Helmholtz free energy F=U−TS,
dF=−SdT−pdV+∑i​μm,i​dni​,μm,i​=(∂ni​∂F​)T,V,nj=i​​.
(203)
This follows immediately by differentiating F=U−TS in the chemical potential differential above. It expresses the same chemical potential through the thermodynamic potential appropriate to fixed temperature and volume.
Consider a closed system consisting of two rigid compartments of equal volume V, maintained at a common fixed temperature T. A valve permits exchange of the same ideal gas; the partition stays in place. Initially nA​=9mol and nB​=3mol, with conserved total amount of substance ntot​=12mol. These are macroscopic moles, modeled continuously, not twelve individual particles. By the ideal gas law, pB​/pA​=nB​/nA​=1/3, so initially
μm,B​−μm,A​=−RTln3.
(204)
At 300K with the stipulated R, this is approximately −2740.311Jmol−1, favoring transfer from A to B.
At fixed T and equal V, integrating the ideal-gas chemical potential gives the total Helmholtz free energy, up to a term independent of the allocation,
Ftotal​=RT[nA​lnnref​nA​​+nB​lnnref​nB​​−ntot​]+C.
(205)
Here nref​ is a positive reference amount of substance; any omitted common term linear in nA​+nB​ is constant along this exchange. Let x=nA​/ntot​ be the dimensionless fraction in A. The relative Helmholtz free energy then takes the particularly simple form
ntot​RTFtotal​(x)−Ftotal​(1/2)​=xlnx+(1−x)ln(1−x)+ln2.
(206)
Its derivative along the allowed transfer and its second derivative are
dnA​dFtotal​​=μm,A​−μm,B​=RTln1−xx​,dnA2​d2Ftotal​​=RT(nA​1​+nB​1​)>0.
(207)
Thus the Helmholtz free energy is a strictly convex function of the allocation for positive amounts. Its unique minimum has x=1/2, or nA​=nB​=6mol, and equal chemical potentials. Initially its excess above this minimum is ntot​RT[43​ln(3/2)+41​ln(1/2)]≃3915.474J at 300K. Relaxation decreases the total Helmholtz free energy by this amount in the model; the final pressures are also equal because both compartments have the same volume.
The beautiful connection is that the direction of matter exchange and the slope of a free energy curve are the same calculation. The entropy gained by redistributing the ideal gas makes equal allocation favorable here. As with chemical equilibrium, a free energy minimum identifies the favored state, while transport properties determine how quickly it is reached. The fixed-temperature, fixed-pressure Gibbs free energy criterion is summarized in 16.4 Free Energy; the rigid experiment instead uses Helmholtz free energy.

Chemical equilibrium

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Chemical potential OurBigBook.com
At chemical equilibrium, a reversible chemical reaction has equal forward and reverse reaction rates, so its macroscopic composition stays constant. Individual molecules can keep changing identity: the reaction has not stopped. This dynamic balance is the definition described by the [ref]. Equal reaction rates also need not mean equal concentrations. A small population converting rapidly can balance a large population converting slowly.
This distinction gives two useful questions. Which composition is favored at the specified temperature and other constraints? Thermodynamics answers through chemical potentials and an equilibrium constant. How quickly does a prepared mixture approach that composition? Chemical kinetics answers through reaction rates. Knowing the destination does not determine the journey's duration. A composition that barely changes during observation may reflect extremely slow chemical kinetics, so constancy alone does not establish chemical equilibrium.
Consider the idealized elementary chemical reaction
A⇌B,kf​=0.3s−1,kr​=0.1s−1.
(211)
Assume a well-mixed closed system at fixed temperature and volume, with first-order law of mass action rates in both directions and no competing chemical reactions. Write a=[A] and b=[B] for concentrations in M=mol/L. The total a+b=C=1M is conserved because each conversion replaces one molecule by one molecule. This conservation is special to the chosen stoichiometry.
The forward and reverse reaction rates, measured as conversions per unit volume per unit time, are Jf​=kf​a and Jr​=kr​b. Hence
dtda​=−kf​a+kr​b=−(kf​+kr​)a+kr​C.
(212)
Setting this derivative to zero gives
aeq​=kf​+kr​kr​C​=0.25M,beq​=0.75M.
(213)
With a(0)=1M and b(0)=0, solving the ordinary differential equation yields
a(t)=(0.25+0.75e−0.4t/s)M,b(t)=(0.75−0.75e−0.4t/s)M.
(214)
At t=5s, these are approximately 0.3515M and 0.6485M. Initially Jf​=0.3M/s and Jr​=0. At chemical equilibrium, both are 0.075M/s, while the net reaction rate Jf​−Jr​ is zero. The persistent exchange is visible in the lower panel even after the upper panel has nearly flattened.
Why does chemical equilibrium also involve a free energy minimum? For a closed system at fixed temperature and pressure, without imposed non-expansion work, stable equilibrium minimizes Gibbs free energy over compositions allowed by conserved elemental inventories. See W. C. Carter, MIT thermodynamics notes, sections 2-1.14 and 2-1.19. This is constrained Gibbs minimization for chemical equilibrium: freely minimizing over unrelated species amounts would change the inventory. At fixed temperature and volume, the appropriate potential is Helmholtz free energy. In either setting, varying an allowed extent of reaction gives the corresponding free energy slope ∑i​νi​μi​, with molar chemical potentials and signed stoichiometric vector entries. An interior equilibrium has zero slope; stability requires a minimum. For A converting to B, this says μB​=μA​.
The beauty of this connection is that molecular exchange, a macroscopic composition, and a geometric minimum describe the same balance. In the ideal concentration model, let x=b/C and choose the standard molar chemical potential difference consistent with K=3. Up to a composition-independent constant, the fixed-volume Helmholtz free energy then obeys
nRTF​=(1−x)ln(1−x)+xlnx−xln3,
(215)
where n is the conserved total amount of substance and R the molar gas constant. Its derivative is ln[x/(1−x)]−ln3, vanishing at x=3/4. Its second derivative is 1/x+1/(1−x)>0 inside 0<x<1, so this balance is the unique minimum. The mixing entropy terms explain why the favored composition still contains A.
